utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Harmon, are you ready to continue the examination of Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Brown, before -- yes. Ms. Loukas, if there's anything you'd like to raise before I remind Mr. Brown that he's still bound by the solemn declaration given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I'd just indicate that in my discussions with Mr. Harmon, he's indicated that he feels that the examination-in-chief will conclude around about the time of the first break. In those circumstances, Your Honour, I -- depending on when Mr. Harmon does finish, I would propose that we take the break when he does finish so that I can be in a position to take the lectern and what have you and organise my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Equality of arms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- things in such a way that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So that I can be in a state of combat readiness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- if that would not cause us an extra break, then we'd gladly agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibits I will be referring to will be in our binder 3, for your benefit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I will also refer to binder1 but that won't be until the end of our examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Harmon: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, do you have binder 3 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to be very conscientious about pausing between questions and answers. Mr. Brown, I'd like to refer you to four exhibits that relate to the massacre that took place on Mount Vlasic. Those are exhibits that are found -- and we'll first of all refer to the exhibit in tab 84. This exhibit, Mr. Brown, is a -- an extraordinary report dated the 21st, and the month is illegible, 1992. It's an extraordinary report that is directed from the command of the 22nd Light Infantry Brigade up to its superior command, the 1st Krajina Corps command. And the author of this is Bosko Peulic, whose name we have seen earlier in other documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He's the officer we mentioned yesterday as commanding that brigade and also Operations Group Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while there is no translation of a stamp that appears on the English version, the B/C/S version does bear a stamp with a time reference of 0800 hours on it. Can you tell the Judges very briefly what this report is.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the report speaks for itself. It's a report of a killing, and it makes mention -- or killings. And it makes mention of around 16 -- 1630 hours on the 21st there was a refugee convoy travelling through -- it was actually through Colonel Peulic's zone and that the police and the CSB were escorting the convoy. The convoy stopped at the Koricanske Stijene, which is a feature on Mount Vlasic or near Mount Vlasic, and there was a killing occurred, and people were thrown into the canyon. And the report mentions that an illegible number of police participated in these -- they call it liquidation. And in fact he uses the phrase "genocide against civilians." He indicates that that his -- individuals from his brigade have nothing to do with it and requests that some following measures to be taken: a commission be established and the CSB be informed, and any other necessary measures be taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if we could turn now to tab 85, and we will be referring to tab 83. What is the document that is found in tab 85? Can you describe that to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is written on the following day, and it's a combat report from the 1st Krajina Corps sent to the Main Staff. And it makes mention in page 2 on paragraph 4 in the situation on the ground -- it makes mention of this incident that was reported previously, that a column of refugees escorting -- being escorted to Travnik, and that a group of policemen from Prijedor and Sanski Most pulled out 100 Muslims and killed them in various ways and threw them into the ravine. So this would indicate that the corps had taken that information from Colonel Peulic and sent a report in their daily combat report up the chain to the VRS Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at the translation -- the English translation on the second page, it appears to have been received by the Main Staff at the 22nd of August at 1400 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it seems to have been sent in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you earlier in your testimony made mention of the corps reporting to the Main Staff sometimes on one occasion a day, sometimes on multiple occasions on the same day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, there are -- these regular combat reports were very frequent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you turn to the exhibit in paragraph -- in tab 83, please. This is a document that appears to have been sent the same day by the 1st Krajina Corps to the Main Staff of the army. Can you explain what this report is.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is another combat report, and I think this one is sent a little bit later in the day, so this would indicate that they -- they were sending two combat reports. And on page 2 in paragraph 3, again, the situation on the ground, it makes reference to that -- that killing, "A massacre against civilians - Muslim men - was committed on the 21st of August between 1830 and 1900," and again it makes reference that there was a group of policemen escorting a convoy of refugees from Travnik, and it indicates the massacre took place at the Koricanske Stijene in the canyon. And it notes, "About 100 people were killed in various ways and left in the canyon." So it would re-echo the earlier combat report and also the initial report that Colonel Peulic sent the previous day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally in respect of this massacre, could you turn to tab 97. Mr. Brown, this appears to be a combat report, a report on the state of combat morale, I should say, prepared by General Talic, and it is to the VRS Main Staff. And in it, there is a reference to this killing that occurred -- that has been reported a few days earlier by General Talic. Could you turn to page -- page 4. I'd refer to the top two paragraphs. Cast your eye on that and explain to the Judges, if you will, how you interpret this.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- the paragraph 4 -- the page 4 in the top paragraph indicates that -- again, it talks about the massacre in Skender Vakuf. It seems to say that there were more than 100 -- over 150, and that Stevo -- I think they've misspelled it here. It's probably referring to Simo Drljaca, who is chief of the Prijedor police. Then it's also -- also makes reference in the second paragraph that this action has caused indignation amongst citizens and the Krajina soldiers. But it interestingly notes that "this dark stain which was created did not have support, but it is very fortunate the international community didn't find out about it in more detail." So although they seem to be critical of the incident, they seem to be highlighting the fact that at least there were some -- they were quite fortunate that the international community hadn't found out about the incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, in -- I'm going to refer to your report --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Which, Your Honours, is found in Volume 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that in front of you, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I'm referring, Your Honours, to -- it's the section -- it's on page 88 and 89, referring to paragraph 2.80, that starts at the bottom of 280 in your report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Brown, in your report, you say in paragraph 2.80 that -- "From April of 1992 onwards, there were regular reports of the killing of civilians." These were reported in the army reports. And you reference a number of locations in the footnotes in your report, starting at 400, and running over to -- through 412, describe a number of incidents where the army personnel are involved in the killing of civilians. And what I would inquire to you about, Mr. Brown, is: In your review of these documents, can you inform the Judges what your assessment was in respect of the army's attitude toward the killing of civilians?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do highlight these are references from predominantly, I think, daily combat reports that identify individual villages or locations where civilians or prisoners, in fact - I think it's not just solely civilians - and these are the ones that I -- I was able to review and -- and saw. There are other more general comments about killings of civilians, not necessarily specifying individual locations. And there are a few of those I think I've highlighted, as well. I mentioned yesterday the incident in Kotor Varos where they themselves reference it as a massacre and then apparently appear to put it down to combat casualties. And as I said yesterday, I didn't see any examples outside the one in Kljuc municipality, Vicici, whereby there seem to be any prosecutorial proceedings, and even in that case, it seemed to dwindle and achieve very little, and I don't believe anybody was -- was -- was prosecuted. I don't believe the military, from the reading of the documentation, followed up on the incidents that they themselves had highlighted in their own documentation. And I can -- from the last comment about -- it was fortunate the international community didn't find out about it, I would come to the conclusion that they -- they -- although they noted the killings and in some cases were critical of the killings, were not interested in following up and conducting any action that would result in the prosecution of anybody as a result of those killings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, let me direct your attention to two footnotes: Footnote 408, which refers to a 1 KK regular combat report that reported that "A group of five members of the Sanski Most 6th Light Infantry Brigade had killed seven non-Serbs, among them three women," and it describes essentially the -- the prosecution history, if you will, in that particular case. And could you comment on that case that's reported in your footnote 408.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually this was one case, again, that did -- when I say it was the only case, I was thinking of it last night, if there were -- if there was other cases, and -- and this has just highlighted that there was one. But I believe this is another case that nothing happened. I think these people -- there was a case file opened, if -- I believe, and -- I'd have to go through the files, but I don't think anyone was prosecuted for this at all. I believe they may have been held for a very brief period of time and nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your -- the footnote says that "The people who were involved in these killings expressed the desire to return to their unit and the prosecutor in the zone of the 1st Krajina Corps agreed to the request and ordered the end of their detention, as there was no reason to hold them." And there was later an indictment, but the perpetrators were never tried.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that was what happened also at Vicici. I think they were held for a short space of time, and they expressed the desire to go back to their units or wrote letters to General Talic saying they wanted to go back to their units, and they were released, and nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I direct your attention to the incident that's described in footnote 412. This is from a report of the 6th Krajina Brigade military police dated the 7th of December, 1992, describing a mass murder that had been committed on Croatian villagers in a village in Sanski Most. Could you review that note and just comment on it to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is another example of what happened. These individuals were held for a short space of time and released -- released back to their units. I believe they even went back to -- under the command of Colonel Peulic and -- in Vlasic, if I -- I'd have to re-look at the file, but -- but, again, nothing happened to these -- these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that, Your Honour, we do have a military expert before us. There are specific documents. It seems to me that questions -- and this has emerged in some of the most recent answers, "I believe, but I'd have to relook at the file" -- I would submit that there should be a little more precision in this is regard, rather than belief from the witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that when the witness says "I believe," that he expresses that he has found no further information in the documents. Is that a correct understanding, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just refreshing these footnotes, I think -- and it has been some time since I was reviewing the documents, not having worked here for -- for a year or so. I -- I remember reviewing some of the prosecutorial logs and the case files, and I saw no - - no examples that I remember now of individuals who after even a preliminary investigation and even being held for a short space of time, no individuals that ended up in -- in those three incidents being -- being sent to prison or -- or in -- in custody for -- for any period of time or brought to trial as a result of these three incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I took a wrong example. You said, "I believe that they even returned back to" -- and then you said, "Under the command of Colonel Peulic." And then you said, "In Vlasic." I don't know from -- from what I remember, it was a Mount Vlasic that the incident happened. I do not know whether was anyone ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a different incident, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the one -- the reference to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But let me, apart from going into further details -- may I take it if you say "I believe" that you are not sure about that, that at least you are -- your knowledge at this moment doesn't allow you to come to any more firm statement in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would argue that, from what I remember of -- and refreshing myself with the footnotes and from what I remember analysing at the time, I did not see in these three incidents anybody being tried for these events, even though they were well known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that. But you said, "I believe that they returned," and then you mentioned a commander, and you mentioned a place. May I take it that your actual knowledge is not sufficient to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that -- those very narrow issues of them returning to the Vlasic feature under Peulic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be less -- less confident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So you're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But in relation to the substantive issue of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you explained that, that you do not recollect any further action taken against suspects in that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, of course, we could have done it in -- well, not we, but you could have done it in cross-examination, but this at least further specifies the level of knowledge of the accused in respect of what he said after he said "I believe."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. But, of course, I have very limited time for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I think it's important that -- that the procedure of the evidence in chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Rather the Judges ask. Yes, no. No. It's well understood. Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, upon the analysis of this page of your report, we can see that you are referring to a certain number of massacres, of killings. You talk about killings of prisoners, killings committed by various people, groups. And I would like to ask you the following question after hearing your answers: I wonder if the military authorities, were they working for themselves in a closed circuit in a way? We're under the impression that those reports are only drafted for the army, without really wondering where these reports will end up. In fact, I wonder now why were those reports drafted, if they were meant to stay within the army, within the headquarters of the army. So my question would be the following: Did you see any traces of any forwarding of these reports to civilian authorities? Because you say in your answer, "I did not see reports," testifying to the effect that there were -- that these people were tried, that they went to prison. But it is not up to the army itself to try those people; it is not up to the army to condemn people, such as police officers, who had perpetrated crimes over civilians. It is up to the army to send to the civilian authorities by way of their Ministries of Defence or so on and so forth -- it was up to them to forward those reports to the civilian authorities so that those -- the perpetrators of those crimes would be tried. So my question is the same as yesterday: Who were those reports disseminated? Were they drafted to the attention of the headquarters or only for the army, without them being sent to the competent authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that most, if not all, of the references to the individual incidents there were regular combat reports that were sent to the VRS Main Staff, in the same way that the reference to the killings on Mount Vlasic and the killings in Kotor Varos that I mentioned yesterday. So those references are reports that are going to the Main Staff. Now, in relation to the issue of the military not trying or dealing with civilians or policemen, I am not a judicial expert and -- but I would agree that -- that there are other competent bodies, police investigative bodies that undoubtedly would have done that. However, General Talic and the military did have a -- a military prosecutorial body, and they did have a court system. And I know that the Office of the Prosecutor did obtain military court records and military court proceedings. And within his own competency, for example, the killing in Kotor Varos of the 200 men, even on the basis of the report that went to the Main Staff itself, it is highlighted that the perpetrators were military. I think they highlight it as the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade. I was not aware of having reviewed the military court records at all that any military figure was brought into, investigated, or went through the military prosecutorial process. I know that the brigade commander from the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade remained as the commander at least into 1993. So -- so that is one aspect. Now, in relation to where did the reports that went from the corps go to, they clearly would have gone and did go to the VRS Main Staff. And as I indicated yesterday or the day before, we are -- were hampered because we were not given access, even though we requested on many occasions -- given access to the VRS Main Staff documents in order to critically look at those. But it would seem to me from the combat analysis readiness report, from the fact that they themselves reference good communications, from the fact that there was a functioning communication chain, that there were examples of briefings, that there were alternative methods by which reports could go up. The police chain being one; civilian chain presumably being another; and there are references in the international media about these incidents. That there were these multiple ways in which this type of information could -- could reach other actors. And I -- I believe in relation to -- as a -- as an aside possibly, in relation to the Vlasic Mountain massacre that there is a reference in David Owen's book, "Balkan Odyssey," that he visited Banja Luka, in fact, around this time in part because, of course, there had been rumours of a killing in that area. And so maybe this is another example whereby, despite what the Krajina Corps say that, thank goodness it hasn't come to the international press, there were these mechanisms by which these types of incidents would have become known. So those are both the limitations in answering your question but also maybe highlighting or reinforcing some of those other communication methods that existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take footnote 412, page 89. Here we see that you refer -- page 90. It's the follow-up of footnote 412. You refer to the report from the military prosecutor's office related to a crime committed, I believe, against civilians. So that was my question: If you reported this, if you were able to find this for that particular case, does that mean that you did not find any evidence of this report transmitted to other military prosecutors for the other incidents you mention? I don't know if I'm clear enough. Why in that specific case have you found or do you refer to the report from the military prosecutor's office, and why in the other incidents, in the other cases, don't you give these reports? Is it because they don't exist, or is it because you did not have access to the relevant documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I reviewed the military prosecutor -- prosecutor's documents, I did not -- I did not see in reviewing those documents evidence on the other cases whereby people were brought through the military prosecutorial process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you had access to the archives of the military prosecutors, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had -- I had access to the records of the military prosecutor's office in the 1st Krajina Corps, and there were some follow-up work that members of the Office of the Prosecutor did in relation to the Main Staff or the army-wide prosecutor's office. And I certainly looked at the records of the 1st Krajina Corps military prosecutor's office. And, in fact, the reason -- if I take it back slightly. The reason we went to look for those documents was very much because out of the 1st Krajina Corps archive we had one report which seemed to indicate that there had been some investigative effort in the Velagici school massacre in Kljuc, and it seemed to me that the VRS 1st Krajina Corps had initiated an investigation against a killing of civilians in the school in their documents. And I felt that this needed to be explored further: if they had one reference, were there more? So we made a request to go and obtain a review -- and review the records from the military court. And in that particular case, the individuals were initially -- or one individual, I think, was initially charged with war crimes. That's why it raised my attention. And I felt if there was one, there might have been an awful lot more. So that's why we went to look for the archive or military records from the military prosecutor's office in Banja Luka. When we obtained those documents, that was the only case in reviewing those documents that I remember that was -- that the war crimes were -- war crimes were charged, or at least initiated. And when you followed the trail of that case, it just petered out in 1993, I believe, and then nothing ever happened -- I think the case might have been reactivated at the very end of the war or after the war had finished. That was the only case. And in these other examples, I couldn't find any whereby the incidents that were related in the 1st Krajina Corps were -- were being investigated at all, except for possibly the other two that -- that are here; the one in Skrljevita [phoen] and the other one in -- that Mr. Harmon mentioned earlier on, I think Carakovo. The rest -- and actually what I tended to find in the -- in the military court records -- and I'm, by the way, not an expert on the military court process, necessarily, or the whole records -- was that there were a number of examples whereby non-Serbs were being pushed through the military court process and charged and prosecuted, and there were incidents where Serbs were being pushed through for attacks on other Serbs. But there was nothing that would link any of these other incidents in the court records at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Maybe one last question. You might not even be able to answer it. These military courts, what was the situation within the judicial system? Did they depend only on the military system? Were they only placed under the military authorities or also under the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would prefer someone who has more of an experience in judicial matters to -- to explain that. I don't think it's really within my competency to answer. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, how do you reconcile the lack of prosecutions and the lack of punishment that you see revealed in these -- for these crimes that you see revealed in the military reports with the frequent or relatively frequent admonition contained in some of these documents to abide by the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- it strikes me as the references to abiding by the Geneva Conventions were not -- were certainly not obeyed and that they seemed somewhat hollow in relation to their genuine nature of abiding by those regulations. And it -- I don't necessarily see that exclusively in relation to killings. There are references to people in detention camps who don't deserve to be there. There are -- there clearly are references to people being moved out and expelled. And it strikes me that there is this very stark -- stark view, on the one hand, where some of the documents do make references to abiding by the Geneva Conventions but, on the other hand, that this activity was going on. And it went on for a period of time. And I can only come to the conclusion that these -- not only were they not -- were they not abided by but they were hollow statements in their own documentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, in the limited time that is remaining, I want to cover two more topics with you. And I first of all would like to cover the topic of the resettlement and the expulsion of people in the area of the 1 KK. Did -- when you assessed the documentation that you had at your disposal, could you assess the attitude of the army toward expulsions and resettlements, and could you also assess their participation in those events?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, for your benefit, Mr. Brown covers this in part in his report starting at page 110 through page 122.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to look at a series of documents in a few minutes, Mr. Brown, so there's no reason necessarily to reference documents at this point in time. I'd just like your general view about what the documentation showed insofar as it revealed the part -- the army's participation in an attitude towards expulsions and resettlement.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the army, from the documentation, were first and foremost very aware of it, that it was occurring. And I think there are references that would indicate that they were engaged in assisting that process and that they operated with the police and in coordination with civilian bodies in order to assist in that process. And off the top of my head, I remember at least one document where they actively supported it and encouraged that there should be -- civilian authorities should work harder at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, can you define in your own terms what "resettlement" means in the context of the army documents that you read.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, before we go on to the next question, we have this indication of "off the top of my head, I remember at least one document." Perhaps it might be appropriate to ask and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to cover that document in just a few minutes. So rather than have a protracted debate on that, I'm prepared to show Mr. Brown that document in just a few minutes, and I am quite conscious of the clock.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm happy with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, my question was, In the context of the documentation you've reviewed there's frequent references, to resettlement. Can you give us the context of what that meant.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think "resettlement" meant either the forcible removal of individuals from -- from areas that they wanted to control or an awareness that individuals, through fear or other reasons, were leaving and would not be coming back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I'm going to refer you to a series of documents now, and I'm going to invite your comments on each. The first is found in tab 88. This is a -- I'll give everybody time to secure their binders. Tab 88, you'll see, Mr. Brown, is a document that is dated the 1st of June. This is approximately three weeks after the strategic objectives were announced, and this is a document that is from the 1st Krajina Corps, and it is signed by Colonel Vukelic. It's a report on the current political and security situation. And I refer you to the third paragraph in that document. Could you -- and this is a document -- I'll read the paragraph very quickly. It refers to "Groups being disarmed every day, particularly in the city." And then it says, and I quote, "A portion of the Muslim and Croatian population is moving out, and the region of Bosnian Krajina has issued a decision to facilitate such departures, providing the Serbs from Central Bosnia in places with predominantly Muslim and Croatian populations were also allowed to move out. Those departing will not be allowed to return." Can you just briefly comment on that. We have a number of documents to go through.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it clearly shows - excuse me - it clearly shows an awareness that people are leaving. It clearly shows an awareness that they are aware that the region of Krajina has issued decisions. So there's a issue of cooperation at least there or knowledge of what they're doing. And they are obviously aware of the issue of Muslims and Croats moving and Serbs moving into, presumably, RS territory, and the reference that those departing will not be allowed to return would indicate some permanency in the fact that these people will not be coming back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, let me direct your attention to tab 87.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it possible for me just to comment on another section of this document?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we'd go to page 2 on the top. This document was written only a few days after the attacks in Prijedor, and they're highlighting what's going on more generally in the whole corps, but they highlight the issue of Prijedor. And at the top paragraph, they make reference of -- actually it's at the very bottom of page 1: "The heaviest fighting has taken place in the area of Hambarine, Prijedor, and Kozarac. Troops under the command of the Prijedor area cleared Hambarine and Kozarac completely and completely destroyed one ZNG unit, black shirts, foreign mercenaries, and legionaires. The troops have arrested more than 2.000 Green Berets who are now in Omarska. 135 of them are in Stara Gradiska prison -" Stara Gradiska prison was a prison that the JNA had used; it's in Croatia, just over the border, and the 1 Krajina corps ran that prison - "and about 5.000 in the village of Trnopolje. Among the arrested is a large number of officers and organisers of paramilitary formations." They then go on to talk about "All SRBH troops in the areas have demonstrated a high degree of combat readiness, with the troops from the seasoned 343rd Brigade excelling. The troops and officers received a written commendation from the corps commanders for their determined skill and courage they have demonstrated. They are an example of how one should act while defending the SRBH," and then they mention that some members of the army had been killed during that fighting and some wounded. And this, again, indicates to me that the corps was very aware that people were -- well, the areas were being attacked. They're commending the very unit that took part in it, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I don't know whether you can have a look at your screen. It says, "Kindly slow down for the purposes of the record."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not only translation but also the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour. And they note that -- well, some 7.000 here, anyway. They call them "Green Berets" -- "are in Omarska and Trnopolje."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, perhaps it's a misreading of the document. I think the document says 2.000, rather than 7.000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I meant 7.000 in total because it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, 7.000 in total.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, let's turn to the next document because I will soon run out of time and I need to address about 15 documents.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we'd turn to the next document. This is a document written the day after this document that was just referred to. This is found in tab 87, a document from the 1st Krajina Corps dated the 2nd of June from General Talic himself, and it's a regular combat report. And at the end of paragraph 2, he says, and I quote, "In the area of Derventa, there continues to be occasional artillery fire while the Muslim extremists have failed to hand in their weapons. The Muslim population of the area of Lisnja village has been expelled." Can you comment on that document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's self-evident that he's referring to Lisnja village, which was a Muslim village in Prnjavor municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn to the document that's found at tab 72. Now, this -- this document is only a couple days after the document that General Talic sent up to the Main Staff, and this is a document dated the 4th of June from the Sanski Most Crisis Staff, and it's their conclusions. And I'd like to direct your attention to the first paragraph, which is the first conclusion, and it says that "Mirko Vrucinic, Nedeljko Rasula, and Colonel Nedjo Anicic shall be in charge of resolving the issue of prisoners and their categorisation and deportation to Manjaca." And the categories that are listed are, first category, politicians; second category, nationalist extremist; third category, people unwelcome in Sanski Most municipality. And then it ends with "In view of this, have a talk with Colonel Stevilovic from the 1st Krajina Corps." Now, Mr. Brown, this is a document that talks about deportation. My first question is, Manjaca, that is referred to, what -- what is "Manjaca," for the record?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Manjaca was a military-run detention camp in Banja Luka municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is talking about the deportation of people who from the categories are civilians in part; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you comment further on this document and its relationship to the army?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware from other documentation that people were transferred from Sanski Most to -- to Manjaca camp. And for the record, Colonel Stevilovic is the chief of security of the corps, a subordinate to General Talic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were those people who were transferred from Sanski Most to Manjaca transported with the assistance of the military?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were transported with the assistance of the police; I think the police escorted them to the camp. And for the record, some individuals died during that transfer. That's referenced in documentation, by the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn, Mr. Brown, to tab 90. This document was issued by General Talic about a month after the strategic objectives were announced. It is dated the 14th of June. It is to the Main Staff, "A state of combat and morale of the units of the 1st Krajina Corps." Before directing your attention to the part dealing with expulsions, let me direct your attention to a -- paragraph 1. Five lines from the -- from the bottom of -- above the bottom of that paragraph, General Talic in this -- reports, and I quote, "The entire zone of responsibility is fully under control." He's talking -- the entire zone of responsibility being his area of responsibility, is he not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So if we could now turn to page 3, the paragraph directly above the number 3 that is in bold, and I will read it. "The most difficult situation concerns the Muslim and Croat refugees in the area of AR Krajina, their security, and the provision of food. The attempt to expel them to Central Bosnia failed because of transportation difficulties and their resistance to leaving their places of residence." Again, I invite your comments on this, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would seem to indicate a knowledge that people are being expelled that and that -- that he's more worried about logistic difficulties involved in that process than -- than -- than necessary -- and also the problems that -- because some of them were having to stay, that it's giving rise to vindictiveness and revenge, and the enemy are closing their ranks as a result of that. So he -- he seems to be not -- aware of the expulsions, and the only reasons that they seem not to be being expelled is because of logistic problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn to the item in -- in tab 94. Mr. Brown, this is a 1st Krajina Corps report dated the 28th of July, and it is directed to the army Main Staff. And I'd like to refer you to two parts of this document. The first is in paragraph 3, which I will quote: "In the city of Banja Luka and other large towns, there is an increased demand for the organisation of the departure of Croatian and Muslim population. We considered that the municipal and regional authorities should work much harder at this." When he refers to "we," I -- do you conclude he's referring to the 1 Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, can I have your comments on this.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at face value, what he seems to be saying is that he's aware of this increased demand for the -- for the organisation and departure of non-Serbs, and he agrees that the regional authority should work harder at facilitating that. He isn't exactly saying that that should not occur. He's not going, on the face of this, disagreeing with the -- what's happening, and he seems to be trying to encourage that these departures should -- should continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during this period of time, General Talic, who was the head of the Krajina Corps, was a part of the staff of the -- of the ARK, wasn't he? We saw that in an earlier document, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not quite sure if the ARK Crisis Staff was still functioning at this date when this document was written, and I would have to defer to somebody who would know more than that. But he certainly was a significant commander, one of -- at this case, five corps commanders. He headed the biggest single corps in the VRS, and he clearly was an important military figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn -- I want to just touch on this very, very, very briefly, Mr. Brown. If you'd turn to page 2 of this document. There's a reference to somebody you've discussed earlier. It is on page 2, under paragraph 5, the second paragraph. It identifies and it says, "Among those, there are officers such as Lieutenant Veljko Milankovic, an excellent combat soldier but inclined to shady dealings." Do you see that reference?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you -- in respect of being an excellent combat soldier, you indicated that -- Veljko Milankovic continued to remain in the VRS despite his -- his shady dealings in this reference, despite his criminal record that you referenced earlier. What's the relationship, do you think, between being a good soldier and -- and being someone of his quality able to remain in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in his case, I can only assume that it was more important for him to -- to be an excellent combat soldier and to assist the corps and that -- you know that -- that his shady dealings were of less importance than his ability to -- to command forces and fight within the corps. And as I said, beforehand he remained in the corps, was ordered to Knin, was wounded and -- I believe -- in fact, I know from a document was also recommended for a commendation by General Talic, so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see, Mr. Brown, in the reports that you analysed the corps reporting on the -- on the departures of people from the various municipalities? And I can refer you to tab number 93.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were -- there were documents which made specific reference to numbers, and there were other documents, not necessarily exclusively military documents, which talked about numbers, as well. I'm not sure if this is one -- tab 93 is one that talks about --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 93, take a look at the first paragraph, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is one example. "Croats from Kotor Varos" -- it announces which -- the three villages -- "are announcing mass departures", and basically from the period of the 15th of to the 25th of July 1.000 people have moved out of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, let -- let me show you a document that you -- it was not in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor at the time you prepared your report. It's found in tab 86, and I would like to invite your comments on it. This is a report that was from the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo, and it was written to -- it was addressed to the president of the Presidency and to the Prime Minister. So it's addressed to the political leadership. It's a report on the work of the Ministry of the Interior, and it's dated the 17th of July, and it essentially reports results of a meeting that was held in Belgrade on the 11th of July as part of an ongoing analysis of the situation in Bosnia. And if you'd turn to page 3 of the document, at the top it reads, "The army, Crisis Staffs, and War Presidencies have requested that the army round up or capture as many civilians as possible and they leave such undefined camps to Internal Affairs organs. The conditions in some of these camps are poor. There is no food. Individuals sometimes do not observe international norms, et cetera." Can I invite your comments as to this, particularly in relation to the military documentation that you saw in respect of the army's conduct toward resettlement and expulsions.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in some of the documentation I have seen that, is very much a picture of what happened, that the army conducted operations, people were rounded up, taken to detention camps in some cases, processed through detention camps, occasionally moved to other detention camps, and there are also additional references that people are being expelled or are leaving or are -- in an organised fashion or being -- are being -- are leaving the territory. So it would seem that this is a reflection of some of the documentation -- of the other documentation I've seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is -- that documentation you saw, you've earlier -- we've already looked at, indicates the rounding-up of thousands of civilians, does it not? I'm referring to the -- the report that we saw that was a result of the commission report with -- from the three municipalities. It identified numbers of civilians that had been rounded up and --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- processed through camps, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And also that other example I've just highlighted, where 7.000 -- they called them Green Berets - they were moved into Omarska, Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm -- we're going to be moving to the topic of camps in just a minute, but I'd like to turn your attention to two documents, please, Mr. Brown. They are at tabs 91 and 92, and if we could start at tab 91. And these documents deal with Kotor Varos, the municipality of Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And for Your Honours' reference, we have looked at a document in relation to Kotor Varos. It was at tab 68. Those are the Crisis Staff minutes of Kotor Varos from the 7th of July in which Colonel Peulic was to participate in the work of the War Presidency. So these two documents also relate to that municipality. One of these documents, tab 91, predates the document in tab 68, but the other one postdates it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see in this document, in tab 91, Mr. Brown, these are the extracts from minutes of the 47th Session of the Crisis Staff held on the 29th of June. And there are two references, the first in item 2, the first subpoint: "All those willing to move out of Kotor Varos are to make a statement at the lower court, leaving their immovable property to the social and political community." And then we get to the bottom of the second bullet point -- the second-from-the-bottom subpart: "Ljuboje Gavric is to make" -- "to take part in the Crisis KS and take responsibility for organising population resettlement." Now, Mr. Brown, what had happened by the 29th of June in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I take you back to that document that General Talic sent out on the 10th -- 9th/10th of June, which was based on a directive in which he in part started off operations in the Corridor and then also to the remaining units, told them to secure their territory. In Kotor Varos, military operation were conducted from around the 11th of June, and they seized control of Kotor Varos. There was some areas where they didn't get complete control, and I mentioned Vicici being one of them. But this comes 19 days after that. And there's the reference -- I've seen other documentation about registering or deregistering the movable and immovable property; I think I referenced that in my report, as well. And clearly Mr. Gavric has been given a responsibility for organising population resettlement. And then if we move a little bit further ahead, there was the document which we've just seen, that 1.000 people had moved out between 15th of July and 25th of July, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, let me take you to the next document, which is in tab 92. You will see once again Mr. Gavric mentioned. This is from the 25th of July. These are conclusions of the War Presidency. And I refer you to subpart 2, which I will read: "Ljuboje Gavric is to draw up and submit to the Presidency" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will say, Your Honour, this appears to refer to the War Presidency of the Municipality of Kotor Varos. Q. I'll continue: "A detailed report on the resettlement of the population containing the following: A number of convoys which have been moved out to date; number of persons moved out; composition of the people moved out; who carried out the transportation and under what conditions, and a financial report including proper documentation on expenses and other important details." Mr. Brown, again, could I have your comments on these two documents quickly because we're going to move in the remaining 15 minutes to the issue of camps.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's self-evident and reflects the other documents that we've just seen, that there was this resettlement and that the Crisis Staff are asking Mr. Gavric to provide them with some significant details about this process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to the issue of camps, Mr. Brown. This is found in your report starting at page 97 through 110. And I'd like to start with reading part of your report or referring to part of your report, which is paragraph 2.106. And in 2.106 you assert the following: "It is apparent that there was significant cooperation and coordination between the military, police, and civilian bodies in relation to the establishment of camps and the movement of detainees to and from camps and detention centres. It is also evident that the military were heavily involved in many aspects of the camps in Bosanska Krajina, even though they did not specifically run them." Now, Mr. Brown, I'd like you to identify the various forms of cooperation between the military and the police in respect of running these camps, preparing detention camps where non-civilians were detained. Can you identify the various forms of co-operation between those two bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I might indicate that I think it's also appropriate that Mr. Brown identify the documents he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour -- again, Your Honour, I am going to be referring to some of those documents in addition to which Mr. Brown has prepared his report, and the documents are identified extensively in these reports. So this is a general question, a survey question. In the 15 minutes I have remaining to comply with that request would consume whatever time I have left. If -- if it will be of assistance to counsel, I can refer to the specific portions when Mr. Brown identifies the various forms of cooperation; I can refer counsel to the specific parts of the report that he prepared. That will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's not --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no question about the report. That's not what my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but you wanted Mr. Harmon not to take the expert to the various documents. Is that what I -- and ask him to identify these documents himself?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I mean, there's been rather a lot of, you know, Mr. Harmon directing the witness, and it's -- it's most unfortunate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What, as a matter of fact -- Ms. Loukas, that would not be a very practical way to proceed. It's clear from the report of the witness that he has documents he relies upon, and the Chamber does not mind if Mr. Harmon would take him to documents and ask him whether these are the documents which would support his findings in the report. Mr. Harmon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Whilst that is the case, Your Honour, there is, of course, the situation that on the day this witness began giving his evidence a exhibit list was produced of documents that were not referenced in his report at all, and I just think it's important to ensure that the lines here are kept clear in relation to what exactly is being referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, what I'd like you to do first of all is just to identify the various ways in which the police and the military cooperated in terms of the detention of non-Serb civilians in the 1st -- in the area of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the areas that are highlighted in the report are obviously there in those pages that you -- you mention: Transportation to and from camps; securing external perimeters, I know in Omarska, was a military issue, internally was -- from documentation was police, mixed security, police investigative teams; transportation to camps, between camps; the document we've seen about Sanski Most; categorisation, coordination there. So those are some of the areas. Providing -- when people were being transported from camps, making sure that there was -- the military had been informed that convoys were travelling through -- through zones; those are some areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in these -- and you've cited to countless paragraphs, the documents supporting those various forms of cooperation in this report, have you not, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've -- I've cited some documentation in the pages you -- you highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I don't intend to ask Mr. Brown to go through extensively, in the remaining ten minutes I have, each of those documents. I can refer Your Honours and counsel to the paragraphs specifically that Mr. Brown, when he has identified the various forms, where he has identified those forms and the documents that are found --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you want to produce them as contextual documents in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I -- yes, I will do that. But I just -- I refer Your Honours to his report. I mean, he -- he reports -- and he's reported -- we've had some of these documents already. The -- the army was involved in the capture of these prisoners. We've -- we've introduced some of those documents already, and Mr. Brown refers to that in paragraph 2.107 of his report. We have introduced documents showing security coordination. He's identified those documents in paragraph 2.109 of his report. He has - - we have already identified documents in terms to the processing of prisoners with the police and with the army; those documents are referenced in paragraph 2.110. Cooperation in terms of transferring prisoners, referenced in 2.111 of his report. We've already introduced some of those documents here. Security at camps; again, we've referenced -- we've identified -- introduced some of those documents, and Mr. Brown references it in 2.116 of his report. And the removal of prisoners from the camps we're going to get to in just a minute; I will introduce some documents. But that's referenced in paragraph 2.131 of his report. But it -- I will continue, Your Honour, because I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- intend to introduce some additional documents to support what Mr. Brown has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're allowed to do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, did the documentation that you reviewed indicate that the military was aware that they had civilians, non-combatants, in their custody?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are references to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to show you actually a document in tab 97, if I can. This is late -- this is a document, Mr. Brown, that is from General Talic and it's dated the 3rd of September, 1992. It's to the Main Staff of the army, once again, and it -- the topic is the state of combat morale in the 1st Krajina Corps in 1992. If we turn to page 3, under "The effect of the political and security situation on the territory on combat morale," this is a document we referenced earlier. It says in the final paragraph, "Certain tensions are still present in the Kotor Varos, Kljuc, Sanski Most, and Prijedor areas because of a large number of arrested citizens for whom there is no evidence or criminal reports that they participated in the armed rebellion." Mr. Brown, can you comment on that paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- it would seem to indicate that General Talic at least by this date is acutely aware that there are a large number of citizens in those areas from which there's no evidence or criminal reports that they had -- they were doing anything in relation to armed rebellion. I would also just for the record like to add that the next sentence reads, "The CSB, especially from Prijedor, is not contributing to this approach." So whether he feels that the CSB are not -- not engaging themselves in this issue, is -- is an area of interest, too, but it's clear that General Talic is aware here that there's a large number of people from the areas that his forces had been conducting operations only weeks before, had been arrested, and that there's a significant number of them -- there's no evidence that they participated in the armed rebellion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, again, referring to your report, page 109, at paragraph 2.133. Let me read part of this report to you, and then I'm going to ask you to comment on it. "The involvement of the 1st Krajina Corps in the eventual removal of those who found themselves in the detention centres is important to understanding one of the purposes of these facilities. The fact that the military were involved in moving out people -- people out of the SRBiH territory, some of whom they knew had committed no crimes, is an indication that these centres were not simply locations in which people were processed in order to find out if they had any criminal culpability or, as was stated -- was the stated purpose of the Trnopolje camp, for example, to protect those who were in a combat zone."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The overlapping involvement of the military, police, and civilian authorities in relation to the establishment and running of many of these facilities and the fact that a significant number of detainees were transferred between multiple camps highlights a degree of planning and cooperation." Then you discuss that many of those who entered the camps were not released home but were taken to third countries. And you conclude that paragraph on page 110 by saying, "These camps were, in essence, a component in the policy of separation in which the military participated." Can you develop that thesis for the Judges, please, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I stand by the statement that I think these camps were a component in the policy of separation. There was cooperation, coordination, it seems to me, between those who ran the camps and established the camps. Many of those people who ended up in the camps were not processed, checked to see if they had an involvement in any armed rebellion, and then released back to their homes. There was understanding that many were not -- were civilians, that there was no evidence to that effect, and yet they were also escorted out. I know in Manjaca, when it closed in December 1992, despite an instruction in August 1992 indicating that a large number of those in Manjaca, there was no evidence and they were civilians, they were simply moved out in December 1992 in buses to the Croatian border according to documents of the 1st Krajina Corps and undoubtedly would have become refugees in Croatia. And I -- I believe that I can only come to that conclusion that the camps were a component of a -- of a policy of separation. I would just like to add, as well, in this regard: At times it's not what's in the report or the documents, to me, that's important, but it's what's not in the documents. And often what is lacking is any -- any conciliatory words or any -- any words that indicate that these people should go back to their homes or should be taken out of detention camps, if they didn't deserve to be there, immediately and returned to their homes, given support, given -- and often it's not what's in the report that seems to be the most glaring. And from the reports that I've seen of the Krajina Corps, those were lacking completely. And -- and what I did see, in fact, was quite the opposite; that -- that individuals when Manjaca closed, everyone was taken away, moved on buses, transported by the military, sent to the border, and became refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we look at two documents in respect of the army's participation in transportation to the borders of different countries. If you'd take a look at tab 98. Mr. Brown, this is a document dated the 18th of July from the Prijedor Public Security Station. It's addressed to the Banja Luka Security Services Centre. Can you please inform the Judges the salient features of this particular document and how it supports your thesis.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This would seem to be an example whereby the Prijedor police are informing -- or there has been an arrangement, anyway, at least with Colonel Arsic, who's the garrison commander of Prijedor and the commander that actually had been engaged in the attacks in Hambarine and Kozarac in May, and Colonel Peulic, who covered the Vlasic-Travnik border area. And it's -- there's been an arrangement that five buses with women and children from Prijedor, from the reception centre in Trnopolje, are going to depart and travel through that area and that there's going to be a police patrol. So it would seem to me to indicate that there had been a coordination that -- and a knowledge that people were travelling through military zones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reference to -- the destination of the convoy is Skender Vakuf. Where is Skender Vakuf, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skender Vakuf is -- is -- is near the Vlasic feature, which was a -- which was the border between Central Bosnia and the RS territory. It's actually near the area where the Koricanske Stijene massacre happened, as well. Although, I think that's actually in a different municipality, but it's in the same area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a group of people who are going from the Prijedor region to be essentially transferred out of the Republika Srpska territory.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's women, children from -- from Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you'd take a -- if we could take a look at tab 99, which is a document approximately five months later. It's in December 1992, a regular combat report from the 1st Krajina Corps, and if we could reference paragraph 3 of that document, Mr. Brown. Can you comment on that, please.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document, as I said, about Manjaca when it closed. "1.001 prisoners were released today, and they were escorted out of RS territory. 413 still remained, and they were due to be released a couple of days later."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you take a look at the final document in the binder; it's tab 100. Mr. Brown, this is a -- a report that was prepared in May of 1993 from the Ministry of the Interior Security Services Centre in Banja Luka. And have you had a chance to review this document in the municipalities that are located within the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I have your observations and comments on this document, Mr. Brown. I note, Mr. Brown, for example, in page 2, the municipality of Kljuc is noted; Prijedor, Sanski Most on the next page; on page 4, Mrkonjic Grad, Srbac, Jajce, Sipovo; page 5, Laktasi, Prnjavor, Krupa Na Uni, Novi Grad, as well -- I'm sorry, I missed that on page 2.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- this would seem to indicate that a large number -- a significantly large number of non-Serbs had moved out of those municipalities and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said known Serbs had moved out of the municipalities ...

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't understand your answer, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would seem at face value to list the number of non-Serbs that had moved out of those municipalities, and there seems to be a significantly large number of them. And -- and this would seem to be a document that would highlight what separation meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no additional questions, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Harmon. As far as document 98 is concerned, you just have drawn our attention to -- we see that there are two originals, one translation. I take it that the English translation refers to the first of the originals presented; they look very much the same, but they are not the same. And I draw your attention to the fact that in the translation there appears to be a reference to "no electricity" in handwriting, which does not appear on the original. So neither of the two fully corresponds with the translation. If you'd please have a look at it and see what can be done about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. And may I just also inform the Court that yesterday there was a problem with the translation in tab 32, which was the minutes of the 21st Session of the Presidency. Mr. Krajisnik's name was omitted as one of the attendees. We now have a corrected translation which we will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that -- I think it is in the transcript that I invited everyone to correct it, and I made a handwritten correction on the original that was given to Madam Registrar. So there's no need to distribute corrected copies any further. We will have a break and we'll resume at 25 minutes to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I see you have two lecterns, so there'll be no reason not to start your cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I noticed that Mr. Harmon had two lecterns, and I thought it was an excellent idea in view of the volume of the material. Of course, that necessitated two microphones. Cross-examined by Ms. Loukas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, firstly I think you indicated on the first day that you gave evidence that you selected the documents that you examined for the purposes of the preparation of your report; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who selected the documents that were given in the exhibit list on Monday that were the additional documents you were taken through?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who exactly selected them, but Mr. Harmon presented them to me about a week ago or maybe not even as long as that, when -- when I met with him before coming here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as far as you're aware, the Prosecution made the selection of those documents.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had no part in the selection of those documents.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were presented to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, in terms of the indictment in this case, I take it you're familiar with the indictment against Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not familiar with the indictment against Mr. Krajisnik. I may well have read it when I was working some -- some years ago, but I -- I have not read it for -- if any, I must have read it once, probably, when I was working for the OTP, but I haven't read it, and I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Preparing your report, of course, you became familiar with the indictment in relation to Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Talic; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I became aware of those indictments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the drafting of the indictments, that is, in relation to the indictment against Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Talic, you were asked for comments at certain stages during the indictment-drafting process; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it you were asked similar questions in relation to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. drafting of the indictment against Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- my recollection is that I may well have been asked questions by that team over the period of -- of their work. And whether that was used in relation to the drafting of their indictment, I'm unclear. But -- but I wasn't at that time directly working for -- for the Prosecution that was dealing with that case, and I was working on a separate team anyway, so I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, you've been working with the OTP from -- I think it was 1998 to 2004; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that time, you produced the report that's been placed before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did it take you to prepare that report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document, I think, may have taken around 24 months, but I wasn't working on it full time. I think -- I think I was asked around about 2000 by Ms. Korner, and the report was finalised in July 2002, but it wasn't the only thing I was working on at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your proofing with Mr. Harmon in preparation for giving evidence before the Trial Chamber, can you give the Trial Chamber an indication of how long that proofing took.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It took place, I suppose, off and on. It -- over a period of about a week. But -- but when I say "took place," I was popping in after work for an hour, coming back the following day after work for an hour, and -- so it wasn't a week's process. I was trying to fit it in with my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how many hours overall would you say?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I -- could I think about that? I would have to count it up. But -- do you want me to think about it now or go away and come back and think about it? I mean, it was -- I think there was one weekend where I must have worked about, say, six hours, seven hours one weekend. And then there were periods in one week where I was doing an hour over maybe four or five days, an hour or two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during this process, you were shown the documents that the Prosecution had selected; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in terms of your examination of documents, clearly a proportion of the documents that you've examined are open to more than one interpretation. Do you feel that you have presented a perspective that is not merely in line with the Prosecution theory of the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll object to that question, Your Honour. I think it's inappropriate to ask the witness. He said he had very little consultations or dealings at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the first thing that would need to be established, whether the witness is aware of the Prosecution theory in the case. That, at least I understand, is more than just what is in the indictment. And apart from that -- no, I think we should first establish that. The question -- I take it that the point you want to raise is to what extent the witness felt free in reporting and in giving testimony to take a view different from that of the Prosecution and how he dealt with that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm interested in his own assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps you --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of his objectivity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we ask -- would it be a good idea to ask the witness to give his view on what seems to be an issue which is now in different ways - with objections, without objection - is defined, which is, What's your assessment on how free you are from any views of the Prosecution on this case, if you know -- at least to the extent you are aware of the views of the Prosecution. Because that's not necessarily included, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe if I can split it into two -- two parts to answer the question. I am not aware of the Prosecution theory of -- of this case. I -- apart from the fact I've been away from the court for some time or the OTP for some time now, and I didn't work directly on this particular case.
