In relation to objectivity more widely, yes, I clearly worked for the Office of the Prosecutor; yes, I worked, for example, in the -- the Brdjanin and Talic case closely with -- with the legal staff there. All I can say is that -- that my training is as a military intelligence officer. My training is as an analyst; I've been an analyst all my life. I tried to do the best to my ability in relation to looking at material and -- and viewing it objectively and trying to put documentation in some context. I worked in an analytical team that wasn't part of the Prosecution team per se; it sat aside from -- from the investigation teams and the Prosecution teams in part for that reason. And all I can say is that to the best of my ability I've tried to be as objective as I can with the documentation. I think in my report, as well, I cover areas that may not necessarily be of direct interest or necessarily directly help the Prosecution; issues of arms that the Muslims had, for example, could be one. The area in the Posavina Corridor where the Croats had conducted military operations to take control of that area, which did sever that -- that link, as another area possibly. You know, I've tried to, within the limits of my own abilities, to be as objective as I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I'd like to return, a little bit more to explore this matter. Just because if we are talking about objectivity, of course, everyone always tries to be as objective as possible in a position where he is required to be objective. Let me just try to give you an example of what I could imagine that would have happened. Quite a number of times your attention was drawn to a line in a text in which the word "objective" appears. It was included in the question often, especially if it was briefly after the strategic objectives had been formulated, that you were asked about a link. Did it ever happen to you that you would think, Well, I see the word "objective," but why apart from the moment in time, why have I not earlier thought of the "objective" here to mean a reference to the strategic objectives? Where, of course, you couldn't read the word "objective" very often, also in a limited sense or in a different sense, a direct military objective. So did it ever happen to you that you were wondering for yourself why you'd read the word "objective" here in this specific way? This is just an example in order to try to find out moments Ms. Loukas might have had in her mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did clearly cross my mind that that could have had far more of a limited reason. But in that particular case, when I looked at not just that document but other references in -- in the directives, for example, when I looked at other references that came out of military documentation, it seemed to me that objectives were not just a very narrow-focussed and small issue that General Talic was talking about. Plus, General Talic is a corps commander. General Talic is of very significant rank, one of the most senior commanders in the VRS. And when senior commanders talk about objectives, they're talking about objectives generally at their level. They're not talking about objectives down to platoon. And so -- so that context, plus the other documentation, seemed to me that there was a bigger meaning to that particular word. And if, for example, in that document of the 21st of May where General Talic says, Explain the objectives of our -- or our goals -- the goals of our objectives, the phrase, whatever, to -- and that was the only reference, that might have shifted my -- my view in what that meant and maybe it did mean a far more narrow meaning. But -- but no, I did think about those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was not whether you thought about it but whether these were moments where you might have had some doubt of where you might have asked yourself: How solid is it to interpret these objectives as the strategic objectives -- as a reference to strategic objectives rather than to, I would say, strictly military objectives with no specific strategic connotation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have more doubt if that was the only reference, Your Honour. And maybe as another example, which -- just away from the objective, talking about, you know, did you have doubts. I had doubts when I reviewed the document that seemed to indicate that someone was being prosecuted for war crimes in Vicici. At face value, had a document that said there seems to have been some prosecutorial process against a killing of non-Serbs. That would seem to mitigate that, well, you know, there was no prosecutorial -- a theory could be that there was no prosecutorial process. And when I found that document, it raised alarm bells with me that there -- that this was maybe not quite as clear cut.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And so when they conducted more investigations to see if this -- to get to the back of that. And I don't know if that is a - - is a relevant example or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least, it answers, to some extent, my question. I can imagine that in interpreting words, Ms. Loukas, that "alarm bells" might have a specific significance for you, which is perhaps also not the only way of interpreting that word.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Alarm bells" could be alarming for the Prosecution, but it could also be alarming that, I have not yet a full insight in what happened, I have not a full knowledge yet. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated earlier that you were in a separate section; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But the fact is that you did sit in on interviews with potential witnesses.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of a team that was interviewing a witness.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a number of cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe a dozen, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what rules did you set in process for your own work in your own mind about how to ensure, on the one hand, that on occasions you were working as part of a Prosecution team and, on the other hand, you were attempting to produce an impartial expert report? What rules did you set in your mind for ensuring that you were undertaking impartial research?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I felt that it was important to try and read as much as I could, for one; to read the documents in their entirety; to try and put documents that talked to the same issue and see what came out of those; to have a process internally within my team of some peer review, and to try and rely on -- on my training as an analyst and a military analyst over a period of time, which was to -- to -- to be objective and to do the best you could in terms of -- of reviewing that material honestly and objectively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mm-hm. And, of course, it's a standard axium, is it not, of proper research that you have to remain open to documents and parts of documents that are showing information that are not necessarily consistent with the hypothesis you're formulating?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I would say yes. I would also add one issue in relation to -- you know, to stating where your limitations are. You know, I state some limitations in the report and, you know, I -- I'm honest that there are limitations there. I'm not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we're just going to go to those limitations now, Mr. Brown. Firstly, as you've stated at the beginning of the report, it's not an exhaustive analysis, firstly. This appears on page 4 of your report. And that it's an analysis of selected military, police, political, and other related documentary material, firstly. And that it's not an exhaustive analysis of all aspects of events in the Bosanska Krajina area between 1991 and 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In addition --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd actually add another one which I hadn't put there, which is I don't speak the language, and so --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that, of course, is very important in terms of analysing documentation.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, of course, I think there are other people in your department who, of course, do speak the language.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Treanor speaks the language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, of course, you don't put yourself forward as an expert in relation to the political sphere. That's Mr. Treanor's area, is it not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is Mr. Treanor's experience, is in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't put yourself forward as a political expert.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not put myself forward as a political expert.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you certainly don't put yourself forward as an expert on the internal workings of the SDS. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't put myself forward as a -- an expert on the internal workings of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nor do you put yourself forward as an expert on Crisis Staffs. That is to say Ms. Hanson's area, is it not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is her area of expertise. I have had some dealings in the issue of Crisis Staffs from Prijedor municipality, and I have looked at certain documentation in the Krajina whereby Crisis Staffs appear to have defence-related issues, and there is an overlap there. But in terms of my detailed expertise on all aspects of the Crisis Staffs and their establishment, I do not put myself forward as an expert there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, at paragraph 1.104 of your report, you've quite clearly indicated that "it's not within the remit of this report to analyse the detailed functioning of the Serb Crisis Staffs, although some general comments should be noted." And, of course, you stand by that. You're not an expert on Crisis Staffs; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not an expert on Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't put yourself forward as an expert on the military judicial system either, do you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have reviewed some material in relation to the military judicial system and -- but it's not something that I've spent a lot of time, and I wouldn't necessarily say I'm an expert in that field, either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, I think at page 15 of the transcript today you indicate as much. You said, "I'm not a judicial expert."

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certainly not a judicial expert. I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- and in relation to military court records, you have not conducted an exhaustive analysis of those documents either, have you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have conducted an analysis of court records in 1992 from the Krajina Corps, but in terms of an exhaustive analysis of all documents, no, I have not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you haven't gone beyond 1992. That's the point, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this report, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in relation to military court records, number one, it's not exhaustive; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The court records are not exhaustive or my knowledge is not exhaustive?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked into 1993 in the court records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, I think you indicated you haven't gone beyond 1992. Are you saying you also looked into 1993?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did look into 1993 court records and -- in the registers that we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But the material available is not exhaustive; correct? You haven't been through everything you could possibly go through in terms of military court records, have you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you certainly haven't gone beyond 1993.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know, however, in the Velagici School file, which we did obtain the records for, that went further up until maybe 1995 or 1996. So there were selected records which did go further than that. But in the terms of the registers and -- and an exhaustive analysis of the whole military court system, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you've told the court you have one example of something that went beyond 1993, but, of course, that's the only example you can come up with, correct, in terms of what we're talking about here, an analysis of all relevant documents?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already highlighted, I think, in the report this is not an exhaustive analysis of every single record or document. I think I'd be still doing that job if I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you asked by the Prosecution if you could highlight for them any documents that you thought might be relevant to Rule 68?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had an ongoing obligation to highlight those documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you select documents of that nature and show them to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For -- for -- I remember certainly for the Talic and Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about for this case?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the collection from the 1st Krajina Corps, for example, was -- was tendered in -- in entirety, and many of the documents that I believe were highlighted in the Brdjanin case as Rule 68 were also passed to -- to other cases. But I think it might be -- I'm not sure if that was -- you know, if I'm the person to -- to answer that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you if -- and the question was, For this case? Were you asked by the Prosecution to look for documents that might be relevant to Rule 68 for this case, for the case against Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a standing obligation from all cases. It wasn't -- it wasn't necessarily one from an individual case or a Prosecution. We were - - we were -- we were at a -- we were very well briefed, and we knew all the time that we had a standing obligation in relation to Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm asking about whether or not you were asked that in preparation for coming to give evidence here.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. Not for this particular -- not during my conversations more recently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in relation to your assessment of your work as an objective and impartial expert, I mean, I take it that you kept very keenly in your mind in the preparation of this report that -- that it's, of course, of no use to a Trial Chamber to have an expert who is merely trying to squeeze every document into a particular overall hypothesis. You understand that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me to comment on whether it's of -- of use to the Trial Chamber or whether --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether you understand that it's of no use to the Trial Chamber to have an expert merely trying to squeeze every possible document into a particular hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Objection to the question, Your Honour. I don't think that's an appropriate question to ask this witness. That's appropriate for a Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm prepared to withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to your work on the text and your footnotes, what do you think a footnote -- what relationship do you think a footnote should have to what's asserted in the text?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should relate to what -- what has been stated in the text clearly, or it should be an exemplar of what is being stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's critical, of course, that it's an accurate reflection of what's contained in the footnote; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it should be -- it should be accurate. It should emphasise what -- what issue that's being discussed in the body of the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's really basic research scholarship, is it not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- it's a feature of a research scholarship, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, of course, a feature of report-writing is ensuring that you're not selective about quotations; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean by that. Taking an individual reference and -- and making a -- a comment on that or -- or ...?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, without reference to other aspects of the document.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you should try to be as objective as you can, and clearly footnotes are there to reference an issue, and sometimes footnotes can become unwieldy if you put everything in a footnote. So you should try to be as objective as you can in the use of footnotes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, it's really important, is it not, that what you've got in your text -- because often as not people don't necessarily go to the footnote. They'll read the text. So your text has to be accurate, does it not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you try to make your text as accurate as you can. Clearly in this report you can't put every single footnote in because you would have a very unwieldy document, but yes, you want to try to be as accurate as you can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go to some of the footnotes, shall we? Let's go, first of all, to footnote 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's unfortunate, Your Honours. I had a little pile of footnote 1s to distribute. But I can proceed without it. They were meant to be in a little assembled pile over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let's go to footnote 1. Okay. Now, what you've got there at -- on page 12 of your report, and you indicate there that "On the basis of available information, it can be concluded that the three leading national parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina, HDZ, SDA, and SDS, have for all practical purposes created the necessary political and economic and military prerequisites to embark on armed conflict among themselves." And you cite there paragraph -- footnote 1. Now, going to footnote 1, there is, in fact, other information -- in fact, the -- the footnote refers very specifically to the war conflict being transferred from Croatia, "The setting-up of Herceg-Bosna and armed formations in the territory of Western Herzegovina: the Posavina, Odzak, Bosanski Brod, and Doboj, Kupres, and the Lasva River Valley, Travnik, Busovaca, Vitez." Now, why did you leave that out of your quote?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would actually like to see the document, if I can, before I answer the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm more than happy to provide you with my copy. For some reason, my additional copies disappeared.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, when you referred to that document and you quote that document, could you give us a page reference?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely. I've managed to locate footnote 1, and I can distribute page 6 of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you like your copy back?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. My question was this: On page 12 of your report, you indicate - and I read out the quote that you've included in your report - you cite footnote 1. There is information -- other information. In fact, the footnote refers very specifically to the war conflict being transferred from Croatia, "The setting-up of Herceg-Bosna and armed formations in the territory of Western Herzegovina: the Posavina, Odzak, Bosanski Brod, Doboj, Kupres, and the Lasva River Valley, Travnik, Busovaca, Vitez." Why did you leave that out of your report -- out of your quote there? Right at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the -- the point I'm trying to make with this document and using the first section of the -- the reference is that simply by the early part of 1992 the JNA were aware that in Bosnia the three leading national parties had, as they themselves say, created necessary political, economic, and military prerequisites to embark on armed conflict. And if I -- I believe this document -- I've only got a section of it. But I think they then go into detail about each three grouping. So they have the HDZ, then talk about the SDA, and I would imagine on page 6 or 7 or 8 they may make some references to the SDS. So it's only taking out this issue that the JNA in one of their own documents are not unaware of the ethnic problem that is developing in Bosnia. And if I put in that section, I presumably would have had to put in the section on the SDA, and I presumably would have had to put in the section on the SDS, which may come on page 7 or subsequently in the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But truly it's important to ensure that right at the beginning you're making it clear that the developments in Croatia have a very real and very important impact on the subsequent events in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I mentioned that in the report that what happened in Croatia did have an impact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we'll leave that footnote. We'll go on to footnote 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, Ms. Loukas, I do not fully understand. You asked the witness why didn't he pay attention in his report to the -- what now appears on page 6 to be the, well, HDZ -- well, let's say military preparations or what they had already; whereas, from what I read in the part quoted from footnote 1 that the expert says all three parties did it. So I -- would you -- is it your point that you would have expected the expert - where he refers to "all three parties doing the same," because that's what it says - to that, "And each of the parties has in keeping with its political concept inter alia proceeded with military organising, establishment plans, objectives and tactics for carrying out armed combat"? Would you expect him to just highlight the HDZ, or would you have expected him to highlight all three parties? Would you accept that, at least in this respect, he left it with the, I would say, more global assessment, each of the three did the same? I do not understand exactly the point you are making. But perhaps I missed some of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it will become more clear when I go to the next footnote, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's part of a cumulative process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, the question that was asked about Mr. Brown's report and why he didn't put in the portion about the potential impact in Croatia is found in the very next -- two paragraphs down in his report. It's discussed explicitly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the witness said already that he did mention that, and I think that it's not appropriate that you add to the testimony in this respect and answer the questions put by Ms. Loukas. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go on to footnote 5, shall we? Now, in relation to footnote 5, you've indicated there that you're dealing with arming. We go to footnote 5, and you say, "As examples, the report on the current situation in the area of responsibility of the JNA 2nd Military District dated 20th of March, 1992, notes that 51.900 weapons had been distributed to volunteer units, i.e., not part of the JNA." Now, if one goes to footnote 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, if you want to tender that page 6, we should assign an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you want to tender that. Mr. Registrar, that would be number D ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D46, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we go to footnote 5, and I'll give you a copy of that, and I've got other copies for distribution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be Exhibit number ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D47, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D47, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we go to footnote 5, you've indicated there that these weapons have been distributed. But if you turn to page 3, it deals with paramilitary organising in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it indicates that "Reliable information as well as the recently televised statements of the Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP leadership indicate that the ethnic groups of this republic are well-armed along the party lines. Muslims, around 60.000 men; Croats, around 35.000, and Serbs, 25.000." Now, you've mentioned in your footnote 51.900 weapons being distributed to volunteer units, and yet you haven't mentioned very specifically what's also contained at page 3 in relation to the arming of Muslims and Croats and Serbs and the very specific numbers there.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's not necessarily the point I was making in this -- in this section. There are -- I think there is other parts of the -- the report that do talk that I don't doubt that the -- that the Croats and the Muslims had armed themselves, and the JNA indicate that, as well. But that wasn't necessarily the issue that I was drawing in the document here. This document I was drawing attention to, that these volunteers had been armed in part by the JNA and in part by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in terms of the proper context, if you are talking about the arming of Serb volunteers, if in the same document the numbers are quoted of the arming of Muslims and of Croats, surely it would be appropriate to include those specific numbers while you're including the specific numbers that you have in footnote 5.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I disagree. I'm talking about Serb volunteers in this paragraph, in 1.7, and this is where this section is related in this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you don't think that it's appropriate to include the full context of arming of Muslims and Croatians when you're talking about the arming of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've mentioned in the document that there was arming in Muslim -- in Muslim areas, and I have mentioned, as well, in the paragraphs earlier on that the Croatian forces had taken control of municipalities in -- in the -- the Drina -- the Posavina Corridor, and that that caused difficulties for -- for the JNA. So I don't -- I don't believe I shy from that issue. And I wouldn't -- I wouldn't -- I wouldn't necessarily disagree with it, either. But issue I'm drawing attention to in paragraph 1.7 relates to the arming of Serb volunteers, which is what paragraph 5 is discussing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if you're going to discuss the arming of Serb volunteers, it's proper to put it in its context when you are quoting numbers that from the same document you have numbers in relation to Muslims and Croats, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, could you draw my attention to the numbers on page 3. Because that's what you said, that numbers appear.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, paramilitary -- page 3, paragraph 4, "Paramilitary organising in the BH."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, what I see there, there are numbers, but these are numbers of persons, not of weapons. What I -- if I would look at it unfavourably, I would say Muslims -- no, just numbers of men and not weapons, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in the full context of the sentence, it is "Reliable information as well as the recently televised statements of the Bosnia Herzegovina MUP leadership indicate that the ethnic groups of this republic are well-armed along the party lines." So it is talking about arming, and it's talking about Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. But then we have 20.000 Serbs, isn't it? On the other information -- I mean, if you try to combine the information, that would mean that if the JNA has distributed weapons, was that to Serb volunteers? Do I have to understand that, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would argue that if you read from the issue of some experiences down, that these volunteers are predominantly -- well, Serb volunteers. I think that's what it's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would mean three weapons for each Serb. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Ms. Loukas, that's something I have some difficulty to accept. So, therefore, I am not fully aware if you are talking about numbers that it's not the same as weapons, and it seems to be a bit apples and pears. I'll try to put into context the numbers. I see no numbers of weapons distributed, and I see numbers of -- I would say of troops or military men, which I cannot link that easily to the others. But if the witness would have any -- or if you would have any further ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Is Your Honour saying that that sentence "Ethnic groups of this republic are well-armed along the party lines" is not a reference to well-armed men?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would not necessarily mean -- of course well- armed men. But I could not compare the number of weapons distributed. I mean, one mortar would do for ten people; whereas, if you're talking about rifles, then it might be different. So therefore, it's very difficult to - - at least in my thoughts - but please convince me if I'm wrong - to combine these figures and to say, Well, if you are talking about 51.900 in weapons, then you should have mentioned also 60.000 Muslims. I'm just trying to understand your point. It's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Your Honour, the situation is that -- and I'll ask Mr. Brown if he has some knowledge of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The JNA was also distributing arms to other ethnic groups, was it not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen evidence to that effect. If you've got some documentation that you might want to show me, then I can certainly comment on it. But I'm not aware of that. I have seen this reference, and I've seen other references that the JNA were issuing weapons to -- to Bosnian Serbs and the SDS. I've seen it in the 17th Corps. I've seen it in the 1st Corps, in documentation, and I have not seen it -- that the JNA were issuing weapons to other ethnic groups. That's not to say other ethnic groups did not get weapons, I have to say, but I have not seen documentary evidence indicating that the JNA were distributing weapons to other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you haven't seen documentary evidence to -- to that effect, that there was at this time that we're dealing with here distribution of weapons more widely than the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the JNA, I take it, Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: By the JNA, yes.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've not seen that. I am aware -- maybe I'm straying a little bit from my expertise, but I am aware of incidents where individuals broke into armouries and seized weapons. Non-Serbs, that is; Muslims and Croats in Central Bosnia. But I am not aware of -- of documentation that would indicate that the JNA were distributing weapons to the HDZ or to the SDA or anyone else, but I have seen documentation that indicates they were distributing weapons to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's leave the footnotes alone for a second. Let's move on to another area. We can come back to the footnotes later. Let's go to All People's Defence. This was mentioned very briefly in your evidence on Monday. What significance do you as a military analyst attach to the concept of All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? In terms of what significance do I attach to it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of examining, analysing the military situation in Bosnia in the period covered by your report in the Krajina area.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, as I said, I'm aware that All People's Defence was, in essence, a doctrine that Yugoslavia had adopted in which the JNA, the TO, and the -- the state mobilised in a time of tension in order to defend the state, and "All People's Defence" meant that, to all intents and purposes, all individuals in the state had a function to play in the defence of that state. The JNA predominantly to defend the borders of Yugoslavia; the Territorial Defence, when it was mobilised, to defend -- well, to assist the JNA, to provide additional manpower, but also to defend key installations or municipalities or other areas, and a process of mobilisation through -- through -- to bolster the JNA and -- and then also presumably civilian bodies in order to assist the defence of the state. That's -- that's my understanding of what "All People's Defence" meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it's clear, isn't it, to understand the events of the war in the period covered by your report that an understanding of that military doctrine is important; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's useful to set some context, of course. It's not -- it's not -- you know, it's not the -- the meat of my -- of my report. By 1992, the situation certainly changed significantly from one way, and All People's Defence was -- was -- as a doctrine was -- was being implemented because of the war in Croatia. But it's of note to have an understanding in terms of the JNA and -- and its -- its function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this concept of the All People's Defence, it was a -- a concept that was assumed and taken into account by all three parties to the conflict, was it not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think All People's Defence was a doctrine that was wedded with Yugoslavia, so I'm not sure that I agree with your point that it was assumed and taken into account by all three parties necessarily. All People's Defence was a doctrine that had served Yugoslavia for some significant time. Clearly, when the conflict in Croatia broke out and then that subsequent conflict in Bosnia, I don't think All People's Defence necessarily applied. And I'm not quite sure what -- what do you mean by it was taken into account by all three parties of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's approach it from another angle. Yes, the concept of All People's Defence was a concept whereby all people in Yugoslavia would be prepared to defend from external attack, firstly. We're agreed on that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And, in fact, in terms of this system, there was a relationship between the regular army, military production, the storage of weapons, uniforms, reserves of food, were actually distributed all over the country in accordance with this doctrine; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. There were these armouries and -- and production clearly was important, and I think the means of military production was split between republics and different locations, so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And each municipality was obliged to have units of the Territorial Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And every municipality had an operational plan for use or deployment of units during wartime.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume so, yes. I am not necessarily an expert on the details of All People's Defence down at the low level, but I do know that the TO was a feature of All People's Defence, so I would assume that there were plans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as far as leadership at a municipality level, part of this All People's Defence doctrine was that there ought to be coordination in terms of war; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, you know, I'm -- I haven't read documents about mobilisation of TOs at low level in relation to All People's Defence, but I would assume that -- that in order to have a mobilisation, you'd have to have some coordination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, each municipality had a National Defence Council, did it not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia began, you're looking at a situation whereby, for example, the operational unit in Croatia, the 5th Corps, withdrew to Bosnia from Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my understanding from the documents that the 5th Corps were mobilised in September 1991 as part of a wider JNA operation in Croatia. They then deployed forces from Bosnia because the Corps was based in Bosnia. It conducted operations in Western Slavonia between September 1991 and the negotiated peace or cease-fire in Bosnia at the end of 1991. It remained, or a section of the corps remained in Bosnia -- sorry, in Croatia and Western Slavonia between that period, December/January 1991 -- January 1992, and it withdrew finally its forces from Croatia, I believe, in June 1992. So the 5th Corps deployed to Croatia in September, had combat operations there until December. There was a negotiated settlement in which the UN appeared. The JNA 5th Corps remained in Western Slavonia on the territory that it had taken and occupied, and remained there and finally withdrew in June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, part of the 5th Corps' zone of responsibility under the -- in the Yugoslavian set-up incorporated part of Croatia and part of Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of the zone of responsibility of the 5th Corps is a slightly confusing -- well, not confusing but complicated issue because the 5th Corps became part of the 2nd Military District. The 2nd Military District was only formed as a result of the withdrawal of significant forces, JNA forces, from Croatia. So when you say the 5th Corps' zone of responsibility in the Yugoslav set-up incorporated part of Croatia, that's not exactly the case. It happened to be deployed to Croatia as a result of the JNA deployment in September 1991. But the peacetime, according to the documentation anyway, the peacetime zone of responsibility of the JNA 5th Corps was exclusively in Bosnia. So it's not exactly correct to say that the 5th Corps' zone of responsibility in the Yugoslavian set-up - if you mean the peacetime set-up of the JNA - that's not quite true. It happened to be in Croatia in 1991 because it was ordered to go and conduct combat operations in 1991 by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we're talking about the wartime set-up here. Now, in relation to the All People's Defence concept, in fact, all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's ten minutes of 6.00. I'm looking at the clock. Another 20 minutes' break would bring us to -- or would you like to take the additional half hour today, since we continue tomorrow? I'm just asking for scheduling purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, I see, Your Honour. And the suggestion is ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could continue today until 7.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you know that we reserve time for tomorrow as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say time tomorrow morning will be plenty, then, of course, we could stop at 7.00. If you'd say, Well, perhaps it's better to use our time today, then I would take that into account when I choose a time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours it would be best if we did have till 7.30. I mean, this witness was in the witness box for the Prosecution for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If I'm even to keep to 60 per cent, that would mean a cyst significant period of time for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm just asking you. At the same time, I consulted with my colleagues, Ms. Loukas. We're now approximately ten minutes in the All People's Defence. I just checked. We have no idea what, at this moment, the point is you are trying to -- I take it that somewhere that it comes to a point where we understand what the relevance for the case is.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, of course, we have discussed before closing Doors. I don't know how much there's closing doors at this moment, sometimes if you close all doors and if there's no electric light, you don't see anything any more. We do not understand how this could assist us. If there's a point to make, we are thrilled to know what that point would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to explain, but I think the message might be clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, the message is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I'm not going to spend much longer on All People's Defence, Your Honour, but I also think it's important for the Trial Chamber to be aware of the background to All People's Defence because it was dealt with so briefly on the part of the evidence-in-chief of this witness and it's a critical part of the military doctrine of the former Yugoslavia, of which all three communities had an awareness of, and all three communities were able to call upon in terms of the way that they dealt with the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. So if one looks, for example, at questions of would-be coordination and what have you, or cooperation, as it were, they're part of a system that was put in place, and it's not part of a system, Your Honours, that just sprang from nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's perfectly clear, Ms. Loukas, that if you lived for quite some time together in the former Yugoslavia, Serbs, Muslims, Croats, and if you were quite familiar with the All People's Defence concept, that that was common to all the three nations or people I just mentioned. That doesn't need -- perhaps for a jury it might take them a bit longer to find out that if you're all raised in the same school that you know, more or less, the lessons that were taught in that school.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But this Chamber is --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is not -- I'm not going -- I mean, we don't have to discuss or to debate your line of defence. I just wanted to convey a message to you. And in view of your response, I thought I would spend a few more words on it. Now, I leave it to you further to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I won't be spending much longer on All People's Defence, and I take on-board what Your Honour has said. But I thought it was a very important part of the background understanding what occurred militarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just finishing up on All People's Defence, in fact, it was - - it was something that was taught in high school, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. I couldn't tell you if it was or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, there was weapons training. You're not aware of that either?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- you mean in high school? Weapons training? Or are you talking about weapons training more generally?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Weapons training in terms of the All People's Defence. That was part of the concept.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm aware that there was a conscript army, that people had to serve some time in this services, and undoubtedly would have received weapons training then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that, in fact, in terms of the military situation in the former Yugoslavia, all reservists, that is, Serb, Muslim, and Croat, all had access to uniforms.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And potential access to weapons.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wonder if you could be more specific, what you mean by "potential access to weapons." Are you ...?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the whole concept of All People's Defence was predicated on the basis of being able to mobilise quickly, was it not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but "potential access to weapons" doesn't necessarily mean - - or can mean a variety of things. You know, you can have -- I'm a reservist in my military, I do not have access to weapons. But when I'm mobilised, I assume that I'm going to be given one. So when you say "people have access to weapons," I know that the JNA weapons were held in armouries, in secure locations. So people as a whole, I believe, did not keep their weapons in their bedroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you're not really in a position to tell us what was occurring in areas where there were significant Muslim majority, other areas than what you've included in your report.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not within the remit of the report and that was not within the tasking. I have not looked at that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I note the time, Your Honour. This might be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if we continue until 7.30, it might be now. But if you would like to continue for ten minutes, that would be fine as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I just wanted to check my documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- during the next break before I proceed onto the next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break until 20 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, I just want to take you to a section of your report that deals with the 16th Session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that commences at page 24 of your report. Now, in relation to your examination of that particular Assembly session, you've taken various quotes from it and also made some comments in your text of the report and also yesterday, when you were being taken through various matters by Mr. Harmon. Now, if we go first of all to, I believe it's tab 44. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Is that the minutes of this session?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. That's the minutes of the 16th Session of the Assembly of the Serbian People held on the 12th of May in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have those in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in relation to this Assembly session, I'm going to take you through it in some detail. First of all, in relation to page 7, there's a contribution there from Dr. Nikola Koljevic towards the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where it's indicated that the Lisbon Conference was suspended the day before.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that on page 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, just in relation to the background to the political negotiations that were going on, you were, of course, aware of the negotiations surrounding what has come to be known as the Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that these negotiations were taking place and that Jose Cutileiro was presiding over those negotiations, but I'm not an expert on the detail of those -- of the plan -- or the political processes that were going on there. But I am aware, in general, that these negotiations were -- were there involving the EU and -- and others. But as I say, I'm not an expert on this area at all, and I'd defer to somebody who is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you tell the Trial Chamber you're not an expert on the Cutileiro Plan but you're aware in general of the fact that there were political negotiations going on surrounding this idea of the Cutileiro Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm aware that the negotiations were ongoing, but the detailed minutia of the plan, I'm not au fait with, and as I said, I'd really defer to somebody who knows far more in that area than I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware that as of the 30th, 31st of March, 1992 stage of the political negotiations that the parties -- the three national parties - that being the Muslims, the Croats, and the Serbs - had adopted a statement of principles, a decision of principles of the new constitutional order for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not. I'm not aware of that detail, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not aware of the process between the 17th of March and the 31st of March specifically in relation to what was occurring on the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm aware -- I'm not aware of the details, but I am aware that there had been some tentative agreement, and I believe that that was then later -- the Muslim side had initially given the impression they were going to agree and then did. But apart from the detail, I really defer to somebody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, there had been agreement on the principles and then Mr. Izetbegovic changed his mind; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness has said he didn't know about the Plan and the details of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's not clear to me, Ms. Loukas. Is there any specific interest to know whether this witness was aware of that or that it happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm interested to know if this witness is aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've gone over that ground. Then he answered that question, that from what he remembers is that -- so he gives you two fingers, I would say, but you'd refer to have the whole hand. Yes. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that there was an agreement to set up a -- a working group to define the territories of the three communities within Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that that was part to have plan, that there had been this -- this attempt to set up a working group in this way, but I'm not au fait with the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that part of the agreement was that the maps of the constituent units should be based on national, economic, and geographical principles but also on historic, religious, cultural, educational, and transport and communication criteria?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it, then, that you're not in a position to agree or disagree with the proposition that the six strategic goals are not inconsistent with the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not in a position because I haven't read the Cutileiro Plan or looked at it in detail to make a comparison of those, so I don't think I'm in a position to say one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in any event, there at page 7 Mr. Koljevic is dealing with the fact that the Lisbon Conference has been suspended, just the day before this particular Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he would seem to state that in the text on page 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Lisbon reference is a reference to the Cutileiro Plan, negotiations.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would defer to somebody else. Whether it was directly the Cutileiro, whether it was another agreement, I don't know, but clearly it's part of a negotiation process, so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go to Mr. Karadzic's speech, which begins at page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, for your information, the English text is numbered in a bit different way from the B/C/S version, because the B/C/S version starts to number again at the -- where the real meeting starts. So since you would like to follow it, please be aware that that might be on page 3, I take it. Yes, it starts on page 3 in the B/C/S. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with the beginning of Mr. Karadzic's speech there, he's talking about the background to what had been occurring with the HDZ and the SDA. He then goes on to talk about what had occurred in the parliament with the outvoting. Have you studied any of the Assembly sessions in relation to what was occurring politically?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I say, that really wasn't within the remit of my report, and I know that there are others who have looked at that in more detail. I -- I haven't looked in that area. I have -- I have made myself aware of some of the Assembly sessions, but it's not an area that I have gone into significant detail, and I'd defer to someone like Mr. Treanor, who I know has worked on that in some detailed depth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your analysis of the 16th Assembly Session is not based on any detailed analysis of the surrounding Assembly sessions; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true. I have reviewed a number of the Assembly sessions when I was compiling the report. But as I -- I said a few days ago, the reason that I focussed on the 16th Assembly Session in part was the army was established then, and that clearly is a defence-related issue. And when I was looking at this, and I had seen some references in military documentation to objectives and -- and goals and operations that the 1st Krajina Corps was launching, I wanted to see if those were in any way related to -- to some political objectives which I read when I was reviewing this document, knowing that the army had been established on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my question was, Your analysis of the 16th Assembly Session is not based on any detailed analysis to have surrounding Assembly sessions. And your answer was, "I have reviewed a number of the Assembly sessions when I was compiling the report." It's nevertheless true to say that you have not gone into a detailed analysis of the Assembly sessions surrounding the -- and leading up to the Assembly session of the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that's correct. Not an exhaustive and detailed analysis of these Assembly sessions. That wasn't within the remit of the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just going on to page 9 of the Assembly session, Mr. Karadzic is still speaking, and he's talking about the further ongoing negotiations there at the beginning, where it's stated: "They, nevertheless, accepted our proposal for a conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina, recognising that the Serbian people would not accept the unitrous [phoen] Bosnia of Alija Izetbegovic so easily, and that is how we arrived at the conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina under European auspices. At that conference, we booked great political success, gaining the approval of the international community, in the case the European Community, for a three-part Bosnia and Herzegovina, as opposed to a unitrous Bosnia and Herzegovina, a complex Bosnia and Herzegovina consisting of three nation states or three constitutive states whose relations and connections would be stronger or weaker." Do you see that portion there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there Karadzic is still discussing the negotiations that had been occurring; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he seems to be giving his view on those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he states there further down: "We have opted for a political, peaceful solution and have accepted the arbitration of European community politics, which does not favour the Serbs at this moment, but we accepted that we might lose a thing or two in order to avoid war." Do you see that portion of his speech there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Now, he also refers to the fact that there was a -- a mobilisation call, further down the page. Do you see that just towards the end of page 9, that Mr. Izetbegovic had issued a mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you direct me to which line that could be? I ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's towards the bottom of page 9. "For Izetbegovic" -- this is -- I'm quoting from it -- "For Izetbegovic, even this alliance, this support, this turning of a blind eye was not enough, and on the very day of Ramadan-Bajram he resorted to a mobilisation call.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. I was looking in the wrong place, but no. Yes, I do see that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know the date of that mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to check, but I think it was around about 6th or 7th or 8th of April. Is that -- would that be correct? Round about then?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm trying to see what your knowledge is, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I know that the justification for that mobilization were the activities that occurred -- one of the justifications were the activities that occurred in Bijeljina and Zvornik earlier. But I think it was after Bijeljina -- the incidents in Bijeljina and Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, further on in terms of Mr. Karadzic's speech there, he indicates that "We have nothing against the Croatian national community in Bosnia and Herzegovina setting up its state or staying in the same state with the Muslims. We do have objections to the cruel war waged by Croatian paramilitary, regular forces of the Croatian state, in Posavina, the Sava River Valley, which have raided Posavina and invaded the Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina, committing genocide and expelling them from their homes in an attempt to gain the best possible negotiating position; that is to say, to limit the borders of its state unit in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, are you reading from --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a different version, a different English translation of the 16th Session? I noticed that the bottom of page 9, I had some difficulties to find it. And when you read it, I now and then observed that you are using different words.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's interesting, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you're reading?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I am, Your Honour. And, in fact, what I did was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not great differences, but I just wanted to check.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, in fact, what I did, Your Honour, was print out the version that was connected with Mr. Brown's footnote in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed, but at least that you are aware that --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we move on there. He also indicates at the bottom of page 12 - and I'm not sure if we're on the same page 12, but I'll see how it compares with tab 44 -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just draw your attention to one difference. You read, "that is to say, to limit the borders of the state unit in Bosnia and Herzegovina," where in mine it says -- and it's not quite the same -- "To establish the borders of their state unit in Bosnia and Herzegovina." So we are working from different versions, but until now without any dramatic results, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. I tend to think not, Your Honour. Of course, I received the tab 44 version on the morning of the -- afternoon of the commencement of Mr. Brown's evidence. And I was, of course, working from the copy that I got from the footnote of his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just that we are aware that there might be slight differences.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we move along through the session, we go to page 13 in my version, which appears to be on page -- the bottom of page 12 of the tab 44 version. It's a paragraph that begins: "We did everything to avoid war and when it did break out, for it to stop and for peace to be established, which would make a political solution possible." Do you see that portion there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he indicates that "The cease-fire or truce has each time been violated first and foremost by Muslim forces in Sarajevo and Croatian forces in Posavina, where the war has never stopped, as well as in the Neretva Valley, where we believe that the Croatian goal is the conquest of territory and establishment of the situation on the ground and the borders, which will, in their opinion, sooner or later be recognised, while the Muslim actually violate the truce in order to suspend or sabotage the conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, just in relation to that portion of the speech, it is true, is it not, that the Croatian forces were in Posavina?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian forces being -- Croatian -- what do you mean by "Croatian forces"? If I can have that clarified: Croatian state forces or forces in -- Croatian forces from -- from Bosnia-Herzegovina? I'm aware that the municipalities in the Posavina were controlled by Croats and that they had taken control of those areas, yes, and I referenced that in the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going on towards the end of that paragraph, there's a statement being made there that "It would be much better to solve this situation by political means. It would be best if a truce could be established right away and the border set up. Even if we lose something, in a manner, the European Community proposes and finds in conjunction with the three national communities." Do you see that portion there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Karadzic there is still talking about a negotiated settlement, is he not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would -- he would appear at face value on this to -- to say that; however, when he says issues like -- one of the quotes you used Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. earlier on, "a peaceful solution," "you've opted for a political and peaceful solution," this Assembly session came on the 12th of May, and there had already been takeovers and some combat operations that occurred in April, and there are a number of references throughout this document that -- in fact, Mr. Krajisnik says it, that "We are at war."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that was a statement of the blindingly obvious, wasn't it? What is the accepted date that the war began, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the accepted date that the war began is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Really?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can you analyse military documents without knowing what the accepted date of the onset of the war is?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure there is an accepted date on the onset of the war. There was activity in March. There was activity in April. There was activity in May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So in all your readings, you say that there is not a day which is seen to be -- or a period which is seen to be the onset of the war.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a difference between a period and a day, of course, but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm happy to hear a period or a date from you.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would argue that late March and April were -- were when combat operations were -- were initiated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's move on to page 15 of the Assembly session, and that is after the strategic goals have been set out. And in the tab version that's at page 14, Karadzic actually -- Mr. Karadzic actually states, "We must also put an end to the Serbian megalomania, trying to include as many of our enemies in our areas as possible, especially as much territory as possible. As many hills and brooks, regardless of whether they are fertile or not, this must be brought to a reasonable measure in order for us to be solid and compact. This can be compared to a balloon which is blown up to be as big as possible, but the bigger it is, the thinner its membrane and the more prone to bursting." Now, do you consider it a possible interpretation of that phrase there that Mr. Karadzic, who's been speaking about the negotiations and continuing negotiations, is trying to keep what is occurring within the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a possible interpretation but one that I would not agree with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to page 16 in your footnote version, which in the tab version is at -- also, fortunately, at page 16. And we come to this portion where he indicates "We do not want to get a state with a huge number of people who are against that state, but that is a possibility they're afraid of. Secondly, we have shown that borders can be drawn bilaterally, and we wanted to move the delineation line as deep and as far as possible so there can be no more going back." Now, where he speaks there about borders being drawn bilaterally, that's obviously in the context of agreement of both sides; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clear in this example what he's talking about and where he's referencing. It could be that he's referencing what they had been discussing in -- in the Cutileiro Plan. It could well be that he's discussing something that's happening slightly more localised. For example, I think he's referencing - excuse me - referencing earlier on Kupres, which I think was a demarcation line, but it's not clear what he means here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what does "bilateral" mean to you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agreements between two parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is it possible that it was part of the negotiating process with the Croats in that regard?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. It isn't quite clear from the -- from the phrase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that the word "bilateral," as far as you're concerned, doesn't make it clear.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the word "bilateral." It's whether he's talking about agreements that they had reached bilaterally with the Croats in the wider negotiations or whether he's talking about, as he mentions earlier on, "Take, for example, Kupres. When we told them we would take their interests into account since Kupres was more important to them than to us, we might agree for the border to run along a road or that something could be arranged. First, by the local armies on the ground, and then by us at the level of the republic." So whether he's making reference to some agreements that he's trying to organise outside of the Cutileiro discussions or other discussions or whether he's talking about those discussions is not exactly clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't he saying that we have shown that borders can be drawn bilaterally?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only re-echo what I've said. He's -- he's saying that -- that that is -- it is -- it's possible to do that, but it's not exactly clear in what framework he's -- he's saying that. One could read the preceding statement that they're happy to agree, at the local level, where it suits them or suits both parties down a road in Kupres, that they'll have a border there. Or it could well be that he's talking about bilateral agreements in another forum. But he is clearly talking or referencing bilateral agreements, and I'm assuming, because the context is Croats, it's with the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In any event, he's not talking about the unilateral drawing of borders, is he? He's talking about bilateral agreement on borders in that context.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He makes a statement that -- that "We have shown that borders can be drawn bilaterally," but it's not clear what he means by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's not clear to you.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clear to me, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We can move on, further on to the session. Now, just in relation to page 17 in your footnote version.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is in the tab version at page 16. There's this delegate, it's indicated there, Mr. Beli. And at one portion there, he -- he talks about communications, and he talks about -- it's about ten lines down: "Until now, we were unable to communicate with anybody, with the exception of our region of Semberija and Majevica." Now, it's quite clear, is it not, that communications on the ground during the period when the -- the war broke out were difficult, were they not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you be more specific about who you mean the communication on the ground between? Are you talking about the military, or are you talking about the SDS, or are you talking about the police, or ...?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you told us a little bit the other day based on the combat readiness report, about this question of communication. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
