utterances.text: And to a large extent, you've based your assumptions about communication on the basis of the combat readiness report that was prepared in 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say to a large extent, but it is a component, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What else do you base it on?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The functioning or apparent functioning of communications in the 1st Krajina Corps to the Main Staff, references to Presidency sessions, indications in military documents of meetings, references in Assembly sessions, the Assembly sessions themselves being a communication vehicle, some indication about notification of the international press. Those are some of the areas that I think I also included in relation to communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the state on the ground in relation to telephones? What light can you throw on that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which particular period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period that you're dealing with in your report.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the combat readiness report indicates that there were problems initially, that they had to rely heavily on the PTT system; the military had to patch into the PTT system, and that they utilised the PTT system. Undoubtedly there were problems. Some exchanges weren't working, I think. The military had to utilise some of its own equipment. But no, there were undoubtedly some difficulties. They are highlighted in the combat analysis readiness report, but they do come to the conclusion that communications in 1992 were assessed as very good and they utilised the PTT system as a means of communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in terms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, may I ask one thing. And I'm addressing both you and Mr. Harmon and perhaps the witness, as well. If were talking about "communicate," you know I'm not a native English speaker. I speak some English; I speak some French. What I know is that "communique" in French, which is exactly the same word, could also be "linked". For example, if you would order in a hotel the chambres communiquantes, that means rooms connected with a door to two rooms. So, therefore, looking at this in the context, I would exclude for certain that "communication" would not mean such kind of a communication as we find that -- and it's -- of course, we're interpreting texts. But if anyone could help me out here because you start and the witness follows you in that respect, that, When we are talking about communications, we are talking about telephones and telexes, et cetera. It's not self-evident for me that if you would use the word "communique" in French, that it would have only that meaning. But I am just asking you, perhaps also on the basis of the original B/C/S text, whether that is how it should be understood. Perhaps we could ask the attention from the interpreters and ask them whether they could exclude such a meaning, taking it from the original text, and then I'd like to hear from you whether "to communicate" in this context would necessarily focus on telephones, telexes, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I take it that the interpreters have followed my observations and, of course, it's -- you're entirely free to consult with someone of your team who speaks the language. But perhaps we could also assist you to draw the attention of the interpreters to the relevant line where you're talking about communication and see whether it's without any ambiguity that the translation is "communications," in the sense of telephones, telexes, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I would indicate that I've given the B/C/S version to my case manager, and I can return to this topic at a later point. It's just in relation to the statement made by Beli on page 17. Or if it might be more useful, if my case manager can find the relevant reference and read it out in B/C/S, and it can be translated by the interpreters on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think on B/C/S it's on page 10, the last portion of -- and then it should then be approximately a couple of lines from the bottom, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the ERN number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I could give you the ERN number. Its last three digits are 725.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, from what I see -- no. It seems that in the original it also says something about -- well, a word that starts with similar, in Cyrillic, similar letters as "communication" in English and "communication" in French.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask perhaps your case manager to slowly read the line in Cyrillic, the seventh line from the bottom. That starts a new sentence. I think that's the one we would need in -- approximately in the middle. Would you please be so kind as to read that slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Up until now, we were unable" -- "Up till now, we were unable to communicate with anyone except for our Semberija and Majevica region. Up till now, this cooperation has been quite good."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That would do. Could I ask the interpreters whether the word "to communicate" here should be understood in the technical sense of telephones, telexes, et cetera, or whether it could have a broader meaning. I'm listening to the English Channel at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the word could have broader meaning, especially if it's used as a noun; the word "komunikacija" could also mean a road if used as a noun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In this case, it's used as a verb, so it's hard to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So at least there could be some confusion as whether we are -- now in the English translation -- I don't know whether "to communicate" would have a broader meaning than - and I am now looking to you, Ms. Loukas, perhaps to the witness, as well, and to Mr. Harmon - whether "to communicate" could have a broader meaning than just technical communication, electronic communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But it would of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've Australian English and American now. So you should be able to help me out.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, obviously it would include those other forms of communication, the technical forms of communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I have no doubt that that would certainly, but the question is whether we should understand it as specifically having that technical meaning.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it's -- it's really ambiguous in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I'm happy to move on. I'd like to hear from Mr. Harmon, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He's nodding slowly yes from what I see, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I agree with the Defence interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that, Mr. Brown, you do not disagree as far as the linguistic version. I know that you're not a linguistic expert, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only that I am Scottish.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Now the issue becomes more confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, that means that the basis for -- well, the assumptions on which your questions are based are not unambiguously established, or the answers of the witness. Let's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Never -- well, I can explore that a little, I suppose. Obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to do that, that's fine. But I think it's just fair for you to know that it came into my mind that the whole paragraph might have a totally different meaning.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, as with many of these things, Your Honour, it's quite clear when one analyses the document that there are ambiguities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I think it's fair for you to know that where you seem to focus very much on the technical meaning, that at least one of the Judges - and I consulted with another Judge - might have a totally different understanding of the part. And I think you should be aware of that because otherwise you might be taken by surprise if that would have any consequences, of course. It's just one line in a document, but nevertheless. It's not an unimportant one. I take it that that's the reason why you're asking questions on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course the question of interpreting the word "communication" as between English, French, American English, Australian English, Scottish, communicating those differences in the word "communication" can become difficult, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going on to a further aspect of the Assembly session. We go to the contribution of a Mr. Dragan Kalinic, which is at page 22 of your footnote version. And in the tab version ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll find it, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's on page 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that -- Mr. Kalinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes -- oh, good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going to Mr. Kalinic's contribution, we get to this point in his speech -- it's in the second paragraph, about four or five lines down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, for you it's page 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It starts off with this: "I would like to address some of the things I have heard here and some of the information and ideas that have been in circulation lately which could create a certain confusion among other people, and maybe this would be the right place to clear such issues up while there is still time. Among all the issues this Assembly should decide on, the most important one is this: Have we chosen the option of war or the option of negotiation?" Now, when you read Kalinic's contribution there -- Mr. Kalinic's contribution, it's quite clear, is it not, or it's possible interpretation of what's being said there that on what he's heard so far in the Assembly session, he's not sure if they're talking about the option of war or the option of negotiation?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he would seem to -- if you -- if you take that -- that line, seem to stress that -- you know, he's asking the question himself, so he may himself have some indecision, not quite sure, and he's stressing his view, which clearly is to have the war option.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's quite clear, as you might expect in any parliamentary session anywhere in the world where there appears to be an ongoing war, that in a debate there will be hawks and there will be doves? I.e., some people that are for negotiations and some people that are for war.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a theoretical and slightly hypothetical issue. Yes, that may well be the case. I'm not sure if you can say in every case, but yes, that could -- that -- that is a feature in some -- some parliamentary states and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So in this session, in this Assembly session, there has been amongst the contributors people talking about a negotiated peace and other people talking about war; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think if there's any possible ambiguity, you might -- might have that with Mr. Karadzic, but I don't think anybody else seems to be, in your phrase, a dove, and Mr. Karadzic himself talks about war. "We are at war," I think he -- he himself -- it's a phrase he himself uses. So I'm not sure that there is necessarily any disagreement that they are at war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, but the point is that he's still talking about negotiations, isn't he? And the drawing of bilateral borders, is he not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he mention it is issue of bilateral borders, but I think I've covered that, and it's a little ambiguous to what he means. He references in the introduction to his speech the issue of negotiations. He does make some references in that. But he -- he also makes references that they are at war, that they've already taken control of territory, that they've got significant territory and hold Sarajevo in encirclement. So I'm not quite sure that -- that he is a dove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't say he was a dove, Mr. Brown. In fact, the context in which I used the term "dove" was in the context of -- well, I might go back to that portion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think the question was: "And it's clear, as you might expect in any parliamentary session anywhere in the world where there appears to be an ongoing war, that in a debate there will be hawks and there be doves? I.e., some people that are for negotiations and some people that are for war." That was my question. You agree with that, yes?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, that in a theoretical question there may well be in parliamentary sessions people who are pro and against conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on now to Mr. -- I think further on in Mr. Kalinic's speech. He talks about -- and that's at page 22 of the tab version. He talks about there being mercenaries on their way from Libya and Sudan and Iran and so forth. Did mercenaries become involved in the Bosnian conflict from areas such as those nominated there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This did not fall within the -- the remit of my report to study this issue. However, I have heard that later in the war that there were indeed individuals coming from other states. Whether they were those states, I have no idea. But it was not really in the area of my expertise, nor was it within the remit of this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether or not Osama bin Laden made it there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't answer that question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, moving on to the contribution of Mr. Vjestica, where he indicates at one point -- and this is at page 26 of the footnote version and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Page 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm much obliged to Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, the portion I'd like to go to is on page 25 of the tab version. And he indicates there that -- in the middle of the paragraph, he says, "80 per cent of Serbs have left Bihac. A large number of Muslims have also left Bihac, and we have a pre-conflict situation there." Now, Mr. Brown, to your knowledge, do you have anything to contradict that statement?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know what was happening in Bihac at that time. I am aware in some areas that there were indeed Serb refugees coming from -- from other areas, and a number of them did come into the Krajina area. But in relation to figures and numbers in Bihac, I'm afraid I can't -- I can't assist you here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it's -- it's clear, isn't it, that in the -- the lead-up to the war that people of all three communities, there was some movement there, was there not? Or can't you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can answer the question in detail, to be truthful. The -- the Serbs that I do know that did come into the Krajina, a number came from Western Slavonia and Croatia. But as to others and when they arrived or indeed what was happening pre, say, March or April, I really -- I really don't think I can assist you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Were you aware of -- or do any of the documents you looked at make it clear to you that Serbs were in fear as a result of what had occurred in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure necessarily that the JNA reports, which would have been the ones at that time, were as quite specific as that in that they would list, for example, I don't know, interviews or whatever. I would imagine - again this, is only just to some extent my opinion - that if people are fleeing from Western Slavonia and become refugees, Serb refugees, that they probably were in fear. But I don't think the documents necessarily touch on that. What they do touch on and discuss are the objectives often, especially come April, March and April, of what it was that the JNA felt they had done in Western Slavonia, which was to protect the Serbs, occasionally using the phrase "to protect the Serbs against genocide." But in relation to documented examples of whether I've seen, you know, interviews or whatever of -- of individual Serbs who were in fear, no, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't discount that that, of course, was -- was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, of course, Croatia's unilateral declaration of independence in June 1991, are you in a position to agree or disagree to the proposition that there was some restoration of the old Ustasha symbols of World War II?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not. The war in Croatia is one that I have not examined in detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there was dismissal of Serbs from their jobs.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would have to defer to someone who's studied that area in detail. I did not look at the war in Croatia. That was dealt with either by -- by others and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That Serb residents who remained had to sign loyalty oaths.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can only repeat my answer. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, to ask for further details when the witness has clearly said that he is not aware -- of course, you might be lucky that the fifth or the sixth that he happens to know something about, but he appears as an expert here.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm happy to move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, it is two minutes to.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I can move on tomorrow, as opposed to this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Or this evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wonder if I could be so bold. I would like to finish tomorrow because I am due to leave the country on Friday for two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we expect Ms. Loukas to conclude her cross-examination certainly by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Do we have a full session tomorrow, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have reserved -- I'll give you the exact numbers tomorrow when we start. I can tell you that until the last break the OTP had taken six hours and 45 minutes, which would mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That does not include Your Honours' questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Does that include Your Honours' questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. No. No. Our questions are such that they should not be -- and they are neutral questions, as well; they are not either in favour of the Prosecution or the Defence. That means on the basis of the six hours' guidance, you would have a little bit over four hours, of which you took until the last break 45 minutes, so you are now at approximately 1 hour and 45 minutes, a little bit over that because we started a little bit earlier than 6.30, which would mean that under this guidance there would be another -- a little bit over two hours -- well, let's say two hours and 15 to 20 minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Does that exclude the questions Your Honours asked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm buying for time here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I have not calculated exactly now the questions we'd put to the witness in the last hour, and I am aware that I dealt with the issue of communication. But -- well, let's say somewhere close to the -- in the middle of the second session.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I might make suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Because if I am going to be confined to two more hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There is just no way I'm going to get through the amount of material I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, Ms. Loukas - and I'm not speaking on behalf of myself but on behalf of the Chamber - that the way in which, especially the first portion of your cross-examination was conducted, is not very much encouraging the Chamber to grant you more than the usual 60 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour is referring to which portion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the beginning. Well, let's say the first 35 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In terms of asking questions about the independence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, in many respects. But we'll consider the matter. But I just do not want to take you by surprise tomorrow morning if the Chamber would, after having evaluated, which we usually do, also the second portion -- that you'd not be taken by surprise if we'd be relatively strict on the 60-per cent guideline.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would indicate that an examination and a detailed examination, for example, of the 16th Assembly Session is critical in relation to cross-examining this witness, firstly. And secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It mainly comes down - and to that extent, cross- examination very much resembles examination-in-chief - that you'd draw our attention to certain portions you, Mr. Harmon for the Prosecution, and you, Ms. Loukas for the Defence, consider to be of significant importance -- of significance and then to say that very often, apart from reading the text - - if you'd say to the Bench, I'd like to draw your attention to all those portions where people are still speaking about negotiating peace rather than going to war, and if the Prosecution finds it important, would like to say, I would like to draw your attention to the strategic goals or to -- where people are talking in terms of war, then the Chamber could digest that information and see what it thinks about it. But -- and it's not to diminish your role, Mr. Brown, but very often it's mainly reading the portion and saying, Is that what it says? Well, this Chamber is able to read. Perhaps this could also serve as a guidance for you. If you'd say at the beginning, I'd like to draw your attention, Witness, to page so-and-so, so-and-so, so-and-so, so- and-so, where they're all talking about peace negotiations, and we'd quickly try to follow that, and if the witness would say, Yes, that's what I read there, as well -- because very often it does not go in any further depth than this.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I must say when one looks at the way the Prosecution dealt with this, that's exactly what occurred. There was reading out of particular portions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying -- I said that it very much resembles; although, it can be done five times as quick as you do it. And even if there would be specific portions, if you would make a list and say, I would like to draw the attention of that and that and that parts, be sure that there'll be yellow highlighted areas, just as good as we do it for the portions of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, part of the reason I've adopted this approach is because Mr. Harmon's approach has been to take the witness through selected portions, and I'm doing the same thing, taking the witness through selected portions that don't match up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- with those particular portions. Now, if Your Honour would say that there is a more shorthand way of doing that, I think that's an excellent idea that should be adopted by both the Prosecution and the Defence and that I'm happy to -- if need be, I can hand up the -- the 16th Assembly Session with the particular portions highlighted. But it's also of use, I think, for the Trial Chamber to hear the witness's reaction to that, in terms of his credibility - and I probably shouldn't be having this discussion in front of the witness - his credibility as an impartial expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but -- yes, but at the same time an expert not mainly in political developments during Assembly sessions. And that becomes clear, as well -- he's not to be blamed for it. But that's, of course, very often what it ends in. You say, Well, this is what it reads; it seems to say this and this, where the expertise is not absent but went to the background. MS. LOUKAS: Well, your Honour, in that regard, I do have a suggestion that will help shorten proceedings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- and I notice we're stealing too much time from the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because we are instructed that if we go on to 7.30, it should really not be later.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, Your Honour. I will make one suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Which I think if Your Honour is allowing me two hours because I did want to spend a certain portion of time dealing with the cross-examination of Mr. Brown in Brdjanin by Mr. Akerman. If we could just tender that portion, that will significantly assist in curtailing the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. But I'd like to receive copes of those transcripts before they're tendered so they're not tendered without my having had an opportunity to review them. I will need to see what portions are tendered so I can see what context they're in and review the transcripts to see if it's a fair submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm not -- I'm not suggesting -- I'm suggesting the entire cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I leave it to the parties to see whether they can reach agreement not only on the principle but also on the technical aspects in the ten minutes to come. I'd like to thank you very much, Mr. Brown, for being here today. But we'd like to see you back, as you may have noticed, tomorrow. We carefully noted that you'd like to finish tomorrow; you will finish tomorrow, and you're instructed not to speak with anyone about the testimony already given and still to be given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
